summary:
- Consolidated, unaudited financial highlights for JPMorgan Chase & Co. covering quarterly periods (2Q23, 1Q23, 4Q22, 3Q22, 2Q22) and the six months ended June 30, 2023 and 2022.
- Income statement metrics: total net revenue, noninterest expense, pre-provision profit, provision for credit losses, pretax income, income tax expense, and net income. Includes basic and diluted EPS and average basic/diluted share counts.
- Market and per-share data: market capitalization, period-end common shares, book value per share, tangible book value per share (TBVPS), and quarterly cash dividends.
- Profitability and efficiency ratios: ROE, ROTCE, return on assets, and the overhead ratio.
- Liquidity and capital: loans-to-deposits ratio; firm and bank LCR (average); regulatory capital ratios including CET1, Tier 1, Total capital; Tier 1 leverage and SLR.
- Balance sheet (period-end): trading assets, investment securities, loans, total assets, deposits, long-term debt, common and total stockholders’ equity, and headcount.
- Credit quality: allowances for credit losses, allowance-to-loans ratio, nonperforming assets, net charge-offs, and net charge-off rate.
- Notable developments and footnotes:
  - Results for the period include the impact of the First Republic acquisition; headcount figures exclude 5,132 First Republic employees until July 2, 2023.
  - Certain measures (pre-provision profit, TBVPS, ROTCE, TCE) are non-GAAP; references provided for reconciliations.
  - Quarterly ratios are annualized; some liquidity ratios are presented as averages.
  - Regulatory capital ratios reflect CECL capital transition provisions.

title: INTRODUCTION
heading: INTRODUCTION
start_phrase: The following is Management’s discussion and analysis of the financial condition and results of operations (“MD&A”) of JPMorgan Chase & Co. (“JPMorgan Chase” or the “Firm”) for the second quarter of 2023 .
summary:
- Introduces the MD&A for JPMorgan Chase’s Q2 2023 Form 10-Q, to be read alongside the 2022 Form 10-K, with references to a glossary and line-of-business metrics for definitions.
- Includes forward-looking statements with cautions about risks and uncertainties; directs readers to specific Risk Factors and Forward-looking Statements sections; notes no obligation to update such statements.
- Provides a company overview: JPMorgan Chase & Co. (NYSE: JPM), incorporated in 1968, a leading U.S.-based global financial services firm with $3.9 trillion in assets and $312.5 billion in stockholders’ equity as of June 30, 2023, serving U.S. consumers/small businesses and global corporate, institutional, and government clients under the J.P. Morgan and Chase brands.
- Outlines structure and key subsidiaries: principal bank subsidiary JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. (branches in 48 states and Washington, D.C.); principal non-bank subsidiary J.P. Morgan Securities LLC; major overseas subsidiaries J.P. Morgan Securities plc (U.K.) and J.P. Morgan SE (Germany); global operations via branches, subsidiaries, representative offices, and foreign banks.
- Describes management reporting segments: Consumer & Community Banking (CCB), Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB), Commercial Banking (CB), Asset & Wealth Management (AWM), plus a Corporate segment; references to Business Segment Results and related notes.
- Notes the May 1, 2023 acquisition of certain assets and assumption of certain liabilities of First Republic Bank from the FDIC, with a reference to Note 28 for details.
- Explains availability of SEC filings (Forms 10-K, 10-Q, 8-K) and other investor information on the Firm’s and SEC’s websites, free of charge, and clarifies that website information is not incorporated by reference into the Form 10-Q.
text:
INTRODUCTION
The following is Management’s discussion and analysis of the 
financial condition and results of operations (“MD&A”) of 
JPMorgan Chase & Co. (“JPMorgan Chase” or the “Firm”) for 
the second  quarter of 2023 . 
This Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q for the second  quarter of 
2023  (“Form 10-Q”) should be read together with JPMorgan 
Chase’s Annual Report on Form 10-K for the year ended 
December 31, 2022  (“2022  Form 10-K”). Refer to the 
Glossary of terms and acronyms and line of business metrics 
on pages 200–208  for definitions of terms and acronyms used 
throughout this Form 10-Q.
This Form 10-Q contains forward-looking statements within 
the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 
1995. These forward-looking statements are based on the 
current beliefs and expectations of JPMorgan Chase’s 
management, speak only as of the date of this Form 10-Q and 
are subject to significant risks and uncertainties. Refer to 
Forward-looking Statements on page 95 of this Form 10-Q; 
Part I, Item 1A, Risk Factors on pages 9-32  of the 2022  Form 
10-K; and Part II, Item 1A, Risk Factors on page 209  of this 
Form 10-Q for a discussion of certain of those risks and 
uncertainties and the factors that could cause JPMorgan 
Chase’s actual results to differ materially because of those 
risks and uncertainties. There is no assurance that actual 
results will be in line with any outlook information set forth 
herein, and the Firm does not undertake to update any 
forward-looking statements.
JPMorgan Chase & Co.  (NYSE: JPM), a financial holding 
company incorporated under Delaware law in 1968, is a 
leading financial services firm based in the United States of 
America  (“U.S.”) , with operations worldwide. JPMorgan 
Chase had $3.9 trillion  in assets and $312.5 billion  in 
stockholders’ equity as of J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 3. The Firm is a 
leader in investment banking, financial services for 
consumers and small businesses, commercial banking, 
financial transaction processing and asset management. 
Under the J.P. Morgan and Chase brands, the Firm serves 
millions of customers, predominantly in the U.S., and many 
of the world’s most prominent corporate, institutional and 
government clients  globally.  
JPMorgan Chase’s principal bank subsidiary is JPMorgan 
Chase Bank, National Association (“JPMorgan Chase Bank, 
N.A.”), a national banking association with U.S. branches in 
48 states and Washington, D.C.  JPMorgan Chase’s principal 
non-bank subsidiary is J.P. Morgan Securities LLC (“J.P. 
Morgan Securities”), a U.S. broker-dealer. The bank and non-
bank subsidiaries of JPMorgan Chase operate nationally as 
well as through overseas branches and subsidiaries, 
representative offices and subsidiary foreign banks. The 
Firm’s principal operating subsidiaries outside the U.S. are 
J.P. Morgan Securities plc and J.P. Morgan SE (“JPMSE”), 
which are subsidiaries of JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. and are 
based in the United Kingdom (“U.K.”) and Germany, 
respectively.For management reporting purposes, the Firm’s activities are 
organized into four major reportable business segments, as 
well as a Corporate segment. The Firm’s consumer business 
segment is Consumer & Community Banking (“CCB”). The 
Firm’s wholesale business segments are the Corporate & 
Investment Bank (“CIB”), Commercial Banking (“CB”), and 
Asset & Wealth Management (“AWM”). Refer to Business 
Segment Results on pages 22-46  and Note 27 of this Form 
10-Q, and Note 32 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2022  Form 10-K, for 
a description of the Firm’s business segments and the 
products and services they provide to their respective client 
bases. On May 1, 2023, JPMorgan Chase acquired certain 
assets and assumed certain liabilities of First Republic Bank 
(the “First Republic acquisition”) from the Federal Deposit 
Insurance Corporation (“FDIC”).  Refer to Note 28 for 
additional information .
The Firm's website is www.jpmorganchase.com. JPMorgan 
Chase makes available on its website, free of charge, annual 
reports on Form 10-K, quarterly reports on Form 10-Q and 
current reports on Form 8-K pursuant to Section 13(a) or 
Section 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as 
soon as reasonably practicable after it electronically files or 
furnishes such material to the U.S. Securities and Exchange 
Commission (the “SEC”) at www.sec.gov. JPMorgan Chase 
makes new and important information about the Firm 
available on its website at https://www.jpmorganchase.com, 
including on the Investor Relations section of its website at 
https://www.jpmorganchase.com/ir. Information on the 
Firm's website is not incorporated by reference into this 
Form 10-Q or the Firm’s other filings with the SEC.

summary: Executive overview of JPMorgan Chase’s MD&A presenting unaudited financial performance for the three and six months ended June 30, 2023 versus 2022, highlighting strong year-over-year growth: Q2 total net revenue up 34% to $41.3B (NII +44% to $21.8B; noninterest revenue +25% to $19.5B), pre-provision profit +71% to $20.5B, provision for credit losses +163% to $2.9B, net income +67% to $14.5B, and diluted EPS +72% to $4.75. Key ratios improved, with ROE 20% (vs. 13%) and ROTCE 25% (vs. 17%); book value per share rose 14% to $98.11 and tangible book value per share 15% to $79.90. Capital ratios were CET1 13.8%, Tier 1 15.4%, and Total capital 17.3%, reflecting CECL capital transition provisions. Memo lines show NII ex-Markets $22.37B (+63%), NIR ex-Markets $13.01B (+28%), Markets revenue $7.02B (−10%), and total net revenue on a managed basis $42.40B (+34%); “Markets” refers to CIB’s Fixed Income and Equity Markets. The overview notes that comparisons are Q2 2023 vs. Q2 2022 and directs readers to the full Form 10‑Q and the 2022 Form 10‑K for trends, uncertainties, risks, and critical accounting estimates.

start_phrase: For the second quarter of 2023 , JPMorgan Chase reported net income of $14.5 billion, up 67%, earnings per share of $4.75, ROE of 20% and ROTCE of 25% .
summary:
- Purpose and scope: Executive overview of JPMorgan Chase’s MD&A for the second quarter of 2023; directs readers to the full Form 10‑Q and 2022 Form 10‑K for complete trends, risks, and critical accounting estimates.
- Headline results (Q2 2023 vs Q2 2022): net income up 67% to $14.5B; EPS $4.75; ROE 20%; ROTCE 25%.
- Revenue: total net revenue up 34% to $41.3B, driven by:
  - Net interest income up 44% to $21.8B on higher rates and, to a lesser extent, the First Republic acquisition; NII excluding Markets up 63% to $22.4B.
  - Noninterest revenue up 25% to $19.5B, reflecting the First Republic bargain purchase gain of ~$2.7B (Corporate) and stronger Markets NIR, partially offset by ~$900M of investment securities losses in Treasury and CIO.
  - Markets revenue declined, with lower Markets NII largely offset by higher Markets NIR.
- Expenses: noninterest expense up 11% to $20.8B, driven by higher compensation (headcount and wage inflation), ~$599M of First Republic–related expense, increased technology and marketing investments, and higher legal expense.
- Credit costs: provision for credit losses of $2.9B, including a $1.5B net ACL build and $1.4B of net charge-offs.
  - ACL build includes ~$1.2B to establish allowance for First Republic loans and commitments; additional builds in Card Services and wholesale (CB) largely offset by a reduction in Corporate.
  - Net charge-offs rose, mainly in Card, as 30+ day delinquencies normalized to pre‑pandemic levels.
- Allowance and asset quality: total ACL $24.3B; allowance-to-loans coverage ratio 1.75% (vs. 1.69% prior year); nonperforming assets ~$7.8B, flat year-over-year with mix shift toward wholesale nonaccruals.
- Balance sheet trends: firmwide average loans up 13% to ~$1.2T (CCB and CB, including First Republic); firmwide average deposits down 6% to ~$2.4T due to AWM migration to higher‑yielding investments, attrition in CIB/CB (including deliberate reductions), and higher CCB spending, partially offset by First Republic inflows in CCB and Corporate increases tied to international consumer initiatives.
- Capital and liquidity:
  - CET1 capital ~$236B; Standardized CET1 ratio 13.8% and Advanced CET1 ratio 13.9% (reflecting CECL transition); Tier 1 15.4%; Total capital 17.3%; SLR 5.8%.
  - Tangible book value per share $79.90 (up 15%); book value per share $98.11 (up 14%).
  - Liquidity: HQLA ~$792B and unencumbered marketable securities ~$620B, totaling ~ $1.4T of liquidity sources.
- Additional context:
  - Pre-provision profit up 71% to $20.5B.
  - Managed basis total net revenue $42.4B; Markets revenue $7.0B; memo metrics provided for NII/NIR excluding Markets.
  - Non-GAAP measures cited include pre-provision profit, ROTCE, TCE, TBVPS, NII/NIR excluding Markets, and managed-basis revenue; reconciliations referenced in the MD&A.
  - Comparisons are Q2 2023 vs Q2 2022; references provided to sections on capital, liquidity, consolidated results, business segment results, and First Republic acquisition details.

title: Recent events
heading: Recent events
start_phrase: •Basel III Finalization: In July 2023, the Federal Reserve, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the FDIC released a proposal to amend the risk-based capital framework, entitl ed "Regulatory capital rule: Amendments applicable to large banking organizations and to banking organizations with significant trading activity".
summary:
- Regulatory proposals:
  - Basel III Finalization (July 2023): Fed, OCC, and FDIC proposed replacing the advanced approach with an expanded risk-based approach that generally disallows internal models (except for market risk), applies the stress capital buffer to both expanded and standardized approaches, and significantly revises risk-based capital for banks with $100B+ in assets, including U.S. GSIBs. Proposed effective date: July 1, 2025, with a three-year transition.
  - GSIB Surcharge (July 2023): Fed proposed revising the GSIB surcharge to use annual averages of quarterly calculations (with daily averaging for certain measures), reduce surcharge increments from 50 bps to 10 bps, and make technical changes to Method 2. Would take effect two calendar quarters after finalization and impact risk-based capital for U.S. GSIBs.

- Outlook and disclosures:
  - Forward-looking statements caution under the PSLRA; outcomes subject to economic, market, geopolitical, competitive, client activity, and regulatory factors. References to Risk Factors and no obligation to update.

- FDIC special assessment:
  - May 2023 proposal to recover DIF losses tied to the March 12, 2023 systemic risk determination: 12.5 bps annual rate on estimated uninsured deposits as of Dec 31, 2022. If finalized as proposed, JPMorgan Chase expects to record an estimated ~$3B pre-tax expense in the quarter of finalization (anticipated 2H 2023).

- 2023 guidance:
  - Net interest income (NII) and NII excluding Markets: approximately $87B, market dependent.
  - Adjusted expense: approximately $84.5B, market dependent and excluding any FDIC special assessment.
  - Card Services net charge-off rate: approximately 2.6%.
  - Notes: NII excluding Markets and adjusted expense are non-GAAP; reconciliations referenced.
text:
Recent events
•Basel III Finalization: In July 2023, the Federal Reserve,  
the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and 
the FDIC released a proposal to amend the risk-based 
capital framework, entitl ed "Regulatory capital rule: 
Amendments applicable to large banking organizations 
and to banking organizations with significant trading 
activity". Under the proposal, changes would include 
replacement of the advanced approach with an expanded 
risk-based approach, which would not permit the use of 
internal models for the calculation of risk-weighted 
assets, other than for Market risk. In addition, the stress 
capital buffer requirement would be applicable to both 
the expanded risk-based approach and the standardized 
approach. The proposal would significantly revise risk-
based capital requirements for all banks with assets of 
$100 billion or more, including the Firm and other U.S. 
global systemically important banks ("GSIBs"). The 
proposed effective date is July 1, 2025 with a three year 
transition period applicable to the expanded risk-based 
approach.
•GSIB Surcharge: In July 2023, the Federal Reserve also 
released a proposal to amend the calculation of the GSIB 
surcharge. If adopted as proposed, these amendments 
would require the Firm to assess its GSIB surcharge on an 
annual basis, using the average of the quarterly 
surcharge calculations throughout the calendar year, with 
daily averaging required for certain measures within the 
surcharge calculation. Surcharge increments would be 
reduced from 50bp to 10bp and there would also be 
other technical amendments to the Method 2 calculation. 
The proposed amendments would revise risk-based 
capital requirements for the Firm and other U.S. GSIBs, 
and would become effective on two calendar quarters 
after the adoption of the final rule.
Refer to Capital Risk Management on pages 48-53  for 
additional information.

title: First Republic acquisition
heading: First Republic acquisition
start_phrase: On May 1, 2023, JPMorgan Chase acquired certain assets and assumed certain liabilities of First Republic Bank (the "First Republic acquisition") from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (“FDIC”), as receiver, for $67.9 billion , resulting in an estimated bargain purchase gain of $2.7 billion recorded in other income.
summary:
- First Republic acquisition: On May 1, 2023, JPMorgan Chase acquired certain assets and assumed certain liabilities of First Republic Bank from the FDIC for $67.9 billion, recognizing an estimated $2.7 billion bargain purchase gain in other income. The Firm issued a five-year, $50 billion secured Purchase Money Note to the FDIC and entered into shared-loss agreements covering certain acquired loans and lending commitments. The acquisition’s effects are reflected in the Firm’s June 30, 2023 financials. Ongoing integration may lead to future changes in reporting classifications and segment allocations. Referenced Note 28 for more details.

- Current market and economic conditions: Points to Risk Factors in the 2022 Form 10-K and this Form 10-Q, highlighting potential impacts from inflation, higher interest rates, geopolitical tensions (including effects of the war in Ukraine), possible market disruptions, government/monetary policy actions, supply chain issues, and other geopolitical risks.

- IBOR transition: U.S. dollar LIBOR’s remaining principal tenors ceased June 30, 2023, with one-, three-, and six-month tenors continuing on a synthetic basis for legacy contracts through September 30, 2024. In Q2 2023, the Firm converted predominantly all cleared derivatives to SOFR via CCP-led conversions. Nearly all other remaining USD LIBOR-linked products will be remediated via contractual fallbacks or the LIBOR Act. Ongoing client outreach aims to complete remediation of contracts referencing synthetic USD LIBOR by September 30, 2024. References prior disclosures in the 2022 Form 10-K.
text:
First Republic acquisition
On May 1, 2023, JPMorgan Chase acquired certain assets 
and assumed certain liabilities of First Republic Bank (the 
"First Republic acquisition") from the Federal Deposit 
Insurance Corporation (“FDIC”), as receiver, for $67.9 
billion , resulting in an estimated bargain purchase gain of 
$2.7 billion  recorded in other income. In connection with 
the First Republic acquisition, the Firm issued a five-year, 
$50 billion  secured not e to the FDIC (the "Purchase Money 
Note"), and entered into shared-loss agreements with the 
FDIC with respect to certain loans acquired and lending-
related commitments assumed in the acquisition . Refer to 
Note 28 for additional information.
JPMorgan Chase’s Consolidated Financial Statements as of 
and for the period ended June 30, 2023 reflect the impact 
of the First Republic acquisition . Where meaningful to the 
disclosure, the impact of the First  Republic acquisition is 
disclosed in various sections of this Form 10-Q. The Firm 
continues to convert certain operations, and to integrate 
clients, products and services, associated with the First 
Republic acquisition, to align with the Firm’s businesses and 
operations. The Firm also continues to evaluate to which 
segments certain clients, products and services associated 
with the First Republic acquisition, including deposits, 
should be allocated. Accordingly, reporting classifications 
and allocations may change in future periods, including 
across the Firm's segments .

text:
The publication of the remaining principal tenors of U.S. 
dollar LIBOR (i.e., overnight, one-month, three-month, six-
month and 12-month LIBOR) ceased on June 30, 2023 
(“LIBOR Cessation”). The one-month, three-month and six-
month tenors of U.S. dollar LIBOR will continue to be 
published on a "synthetic" basis, which will allow market 
participants to use such rates for certain legacy LIBOR-
linked contracts through September 30, 2024.
In the second quarter of 2023, the Firm successfully 
converted predominantly all of its cleared derivatives 
contracts linked to U.S. dollar LIBOR to the Secured 
Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR) as part of initiatives by the 
principal central counterparties (“CCPs”) to convert cleared 
derivatives prior to LIBOR Cessation. Nearly all of the Firm’s 
other U.S. dollar LIBOR-linked products that remained 
outstanding at LIBOR Cessation will be remediated through 
contractual fallback provisions or through the framework 
provided by the Adjustable Interest Rate (LIBOR) Act 
(“LIBOR Act”). The Firm continues its client outreach 
activities with respect to the limited amount of  contracts 
that continue to reference “synthetic” U.S. dollar LIBOR in 
order to complete remediation by September 30, 2024.

- Scope: Comparative discussion of JPMorgan Chase’s consolidated results for the three and six months ended June 30, 2023 vs. 2022; segment-specific drivers addressed in segment sections; references to critical accounting estimates and non-GAAP measures.

- Headline results:
  - Q2 2023: Noninterest revenue $19.5B (+25%); Net interest income (NII) $21.8B (+44%); Total net revenue $41.3B (+34%).
  - H1 2023: Noninterest revenue $37.2B (+15%); NII $42.5B (+47%); Total net revenue $79.7B (+30%).

- Quarterly (Q2 2023 vs. Q2 2022) revenue line drivers:
  - Investment banking fees: Down 5%; lower advisory amid weaker deal activity; largely offset by higher equity underwriting (more convertible and follow-on offerings as volatility eased).
  - Principal transactions: Up 38%; stronger Equity Markets (Prime Finance) and Fixed Income Markets (Securitized Products, Fixed Income Financing); absence of prior-year bridge financing markdowns; Credit Adjustments & Other swung to a gain; higher Treasury & CIO cash deployment revenue; partly offset by weaker Rates and Currencies & Emerging Markets and losses on legacy private equity in Corporate. Markets principal transactions gains were more than offset by lower Markets NII due to higher funding costs; performance is assessed on total net revenue.
  - Lending- and deposit-related fees: Down 2%; lower cash management fees from higher client earnings credits; partly offset by higher lending-related fees tied to the First Republic acquisition in AWM and CCB.
  - Asset management fees: Up 7%; higher management fees on strong AWM net inflows and First Republic impact in CCB.
  - Commissions and other fees: Flat.
  - Investment securities losses: Larger losses from sales of U.S. Treasuries and agency MBS tied to portfolio repositioning in Treasury & CIO.
  - Mortgage fees and related income: Down 26%; lower production volumes and lower net servicing revenue.
  - Card income: Down 3%; higher rewards liability from program term changes reduced net interchange; partly offset by stronger Commercial Card in CIB and CB.
  - Other income: Up sharply (includes a $2.7B estimated bargain purchase gain from the First Republic acquisition); also benefited from absence of prior-year Payments equity investment losses and net investment hedges in Treasury & CIO; partially offset by lower auto operating lease income and absence of a prior-year CB equity-method gain.

- Year-to-date (H1 2023 vs. H1 2022) revenue line drivers:
  - Investment banking fees: Down 12%; lower debt underwriting (weaker acquisition financing) and lower advisory; partly offset by higher equity underwriting (more convertibles and Q2 follow-ons).
  - Principal transactions: Up 44%; stronger Fixed Income (Securitized Products, Fixed Income Financing) and Equity Markets (Prime Finance); improved Credit Adjustments & Other vs. prior-year losses; higher Treasury & CIO cash deployment revenue; Markets principal transactions strength more than offset by lower Markets NII from higher funding costs.
  - Lending- and deposit-related fees: Down 7%; lower cash management fees from higher client earnings credits; partly offset by First Republic-driven lending-related fees in AWM and CCB.
  - Asset management fees: Up 1%; increase driven by First Republic impact in CCB; AWM roughly flat as market declines were offset by fewer money fund fee waivers and net inflows.
  - Commissions and other fees: Flat.
  - Investment securities losses: Higher losses from sales of Treasuries and agency MBS as portfolios were repositioned in both periods in Treasury & CIO.
  - Mortgage fees and related income: Down 40%; lower production volumes and lower servicing revenue (including lower MSR risk management gains).
  - Card income: Up 10%; higher payments-related revenue (Commercial Card growth in CIB and CB); CCB net interchange roughly flat—Q1 partner payments benefit from a tax refund on airline miles offset by higher rewards liability from program changes.
  - Other income: Higher, driven by the $2.7B First Republic bargain purchase gain, net investment hedges in Treasury & CIO, and a $339M gain in AWM from stepping up its CIFM stake; partially offset by lower auto lease income, absence of prior-year insurance settlement and CB equity-method gain, and lower gains on certain Corporate investments.

- Net interest income and balance/yield metrics:
  - NII increased in both periods primarily from higher rates, with additional contributions from the First Republic acquisition (and higher revolving Card balances YTD); partially offset by lower Markets NII and lower average deposits.
  - Average interest-earning assets: $3.3T (Q2 down $42B; H1 down $113B).
  - Yield on interest-earning assets: 5.01% in Q2 (+279 bps); 4.85% YTD (+281 bps).
  - Net yield on these assets (FTE): 2.62% in Q2 (+82 bps); 2.63% YTD (+89 bps).
  - Net yield excluding Markets (non-GAAP): 3.83% in Q2 (+157 bps); 3.82% YTD (+171 bps).

- Notable one-time/transactional items:
  - Estimated $2.7B bargain purchase gain from the First Republic acquisition (recorded in Corporate) materially lifted Other income.
  - Investment securities portfolio repositioning in Treasury & CIO drove elevated realized losses.
  - Markets results show offsets between principal transactions and NII; firm evaluates Markets on total net revenue.

title: Consolidated balance sheets analysis
heading: Consolidated balance sheets analysis
start_phrase: The following is a discussion of the significant changes between J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 3, and D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 2.
summary:
- Purpose and scope: Analysis of significant changes in the consolidated balance sheet between June 30, 2023 and December 31, 2022; total assets up 6% to $3.87T, total liabilities up 5% to $3.56T, and stockholders’ equity up 7% to $312.5B. Major drivers include the First Republic acquisition, client-driven Markets activity, portfolio repositioning, and the higher-rate environment.

Assets
- Cash and due from banks and deposits with banks: Declined due to First Republic-related repayments and FDIC payments, and CIB Markets activity; balances reflect excess cash placed with central banks.
- Federal funds sold and securities purchased under resale agreements: Increased on a lower level of netting in Markets.
- Securities borrowed: Decreased on lower client-driven activity and demand to cover shorts.
- Trading assets: Rose 40% on higher debt and equity instruments to support client market-making and a rebound from seasonally low year-end levels.
- Investment securities (AFS and HTM): Net decline driven by paydowns, maturities, and net sales, and transfers between HTM and AFS; partially offset by $25.8B of securities from the First Republic acquisition.
- Loans: Increased (gross +14%; net +15%), primarily from ~$150B of First Republic loans (in CCB, CB, AWM), Card revolving growth normalizing toward pre-pandemic levels, and higher CB revolver use and originations; partially offset by lower AWM securities-based lending.
- Allowance for loan losses: Increased due to $1.8B net additions (wholesale downgrades and office CRE assumptions; higher weighting of adverse scenarios; consumer additions tied to Card growth and a macro outlook with U.S. unemployment peaking in 3Q24), plus $1.1B for First Republic loans; partially offset by a $587M reduction from adoption of new TDR guidance. Allowance for lending-related commitments had a $196M net reduction, including a $97M addition for First Republic.
- Accrued interest and accounts receivable: Decreased on lower Markets client receivables.
- Premises and equipment: Increased from First Republic lease right-of-use assets and headquarters construction-in-process.
- Goodwill, MSRs, and other intangibles: Increased due to acquiring the remaining 51% of CIFM and core deposit intangibles from First Republic.
- Other assets: Decreased on lower cash collateral posted to CCPs.

Liabilities
- Deposits: Up 3% driven by CIB client inflows and structured note issuances, $68B of deposits from First Republic in CCB, and Corporate growth from international consumer initiatives; partially offset by AWM migration to higher-yielding investments and CB attrition (largely offset by 1Q23 inflows amid market disruptions).
- Federal funds purchased and securities loaned or sold under repurchase agreements: Up 31% on higher secured financing of trading assets and lower netting in Markets.
- Short-term borrowings: Down 7% due to lower Markets financing needs, partially offset by short-term FHLB advances tied to the First Republic acquisition.
- Trading liabilities: Flat.
- Accounts payable and other liabilities: Down 4% on lower Markets client payables.
- Beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs: Up 56% due to higher third-party holdings of multi-seller conduit commercial paper and increased conduit loans in CIB.
- Long-term debt: Up 23% reflecting the First Republic-related Purchase Money Note issued to the FDIC and $25B of FHLB advances, partially offset by maturities and redemptions.

summary:
- Scope: Analysis of consolidated cash flows for the six months ended June 30, 2023 and 2022.
- Summary of cash flows (in millions):
  - Operating activities: used $(92,376) in 2023 vs. provided $24,101 in 2022.
  - Investing activities: provided $5,551 in 2023 vs. used $(125,811) in 2022.
  - Financing activities: provided $14,642 in 2023 vs. $48,970 in 2022.
  - Effect of exchange rates: +$72 in 2023 vs. $(18,834) in 2022.
  - Net decrease in cash and bank deposits: $(72,111) in 2023 vs. $(71,574) in 2022.
- Key drivers:
  - Operating activities:
    - 2023: Cash use driven by higher trading assets and lower accounts payable; partially offset by lower other assets, securities borrowed, accrued interest, and accounts receivable.
    - 2022: Cash provided by higher accounts payable and other liabilities, trading liabilities, and net proceeds from loans held-for-sale; offset by higher trading assets and accrued interest/accounts receivable.
  - Investing activities:
    - 2023: Cash provided by net proceeds from investment securities; largely offset by higher net loan originations, higher securities purchased under resale agreements, and cash used for the First Republic acquisition.
    - 2022: Cash used for higher securities purchased under resale agreements, net loan originations, and net purchases of investment securities.
  - Financing activities:
    - 2023: Cash provided by higher securities loaned or sold under repurchase agreements; largely offset by net deposit activity (including repayment of consortium deposits linked to the First Republic acquisition) and net payments on long- and short-term borrowings.
    - 2022: Cash provided by higher securities loaned or sold under repurchase agreements and net proceeds from long- and short-term borrowings.
  - Both periods: Cash used for common stock repurchases and dividends on common and preferred stock.
- References: Points to related sections on balance sheet analysis, capital and liquidity risk management, and detailed cash flow statements in the Form 10-Q and the 2022 Form 10-K.

heading: EXPLANATION AND RECONCILIATION OF THE FIRM’S USE OF NON-GAAP FINANCIAL MEASURES
start_phrase: The Firm prepares its Consolidated Financial Statements in accordance with U.S. GAAP and this presentation is referred to as “reported” basis; these financial statements appear on pages 96-100 .
summary:
- Purpose: Explains JPMorgan Chase’s use of non-GAAP financial measures alongside U.S. GAAP “reported” results and provides reconciliations to a “managed” (FTE) basis.
- Non-GAAP measures defined: 
  - Firmwide managed (FTE) results and overhead ratio
  - Pre-provision profit (revenue minus noninterest expense)
  - Net interest income (NII), net yield, and noninterest revenue excluding Markets
  - Tangible common equity (TCE), return on TCE (ROTCE), and tangible book value per share (TBVPS)
  - Adjusted expense (excludes Firmwide legal expense)
  - Allowance for loan losses to loans retained (excluding trade finance and conduits)
- References: Points readers to the firm’s 2022 Form 10-K (pages 58–60) for further discussion of non-GAAP measures.
- Reconciliations (Reported to Managed/FTE):
  - Q2 2023 vs Q2 2022:
    - Total net revenue (managed): $42.4B vs $31.6B
    - Pre-provision profit (managed): $21.6B vs $12.9B
    - Overhead ratio (managed): 49% vs 59% (NM for reported)
    - Net income: $14.5B vs $8.6B (unchanged by FTE)
    - FTE adjustments primarily in CIB, CB, and Corporate
  - 1H 2023 vs 1H 2022:
    - Total net revenue (managed): $81.7B vs $63.2B
    - Pre-provision profit (managed): $40.8B vs $25.3B
    - Overhead ratio (managed): 50% vs 60%
    - Net income: $27.1B vs $16.9B
- NII, net yield, and noninterest revenue excluding Markets:
  - NII (managed) growth: +44% in Q2 and +46% YTD
  - Markets NII negative in 2023; net yield on average interest-earning assets up to 2.62% (Q2) from 1.80% YoY
  - Net yield excluding Markets: 3.83% (Q2) vs 2.26% YoY; 3.82% YTD vs 2.11% YoY
  - Noninterest revenue excluding Markets: up 28% in Q2; up 8% YTD
  - Total Markets net revenue: down 10% in Q2; down 7% YTD
- TCE reconciliation and key capital metrics:
  - TCE calculation: deduct goodwill and other intangibles from common equity; add certain deferred tax liabilities
  - TCE period-end: $232.2B at 6/30/23 vs $214.6B at 12/31/22
  - ROTCE: 25% for Q2 2023; 24% YTD 2023
  - TBVPS: $79.90 at 6/30/23 vs $73.12 at 12/31/22
  - Notes treatment of deferred tax liabilities in TCE calculation

summary:
Description of business segment reporting methodology
Results of the business segments are intended to present 
each segment as if it were a stand-alone business. The 
management reporting process that derives business 
segment results includes the allocation of certain income 
and expense items. The Firm periodically assesses the 
assumptions, methodologies and reporting classifications 
used for segment reporting, and further refinements may 
be implemented in future periods. The Firm also assesses 
the level of capital required for each LOB on at least an 
annual basis. The Firm’s LOBs also provide various business 
metrics which are utilized by the Firm and its investors and 
analysts in assessing performance.
text:
Description of business segment reporting methodology
Results of the business segments are intended to present 
each segment as if it were a stand-alone business. The 
management reporting process that derives business 
segment results includes the allocation of certain income 
and expense items. The Firm periodically assesses the 
assumptions, methodologies and reporting classifications 
used for segment reporting, and further refinements may 
be implemented in future periods. The Firm also assesses 
the level of capital required for each LOB on at least an 
annual basis. The Firm’s LOBs also provide various business 
metrics which are utilized by the Firm and its investors and 
analysts in assessing performance.

title: Revenue sharing
heading: Revenue sharing
start_phrase: When business segments join efforts to sell products and services to the Firm’s clients and customers, the participating business segments may agree to share revenue from those transactions.
summary:
- The firm manages and reports performance by lines of business (LOBs): Consumer & Community Banking, Corporate & Investment Bank, Commercial Banking, and Asset & Wealth Management, plus a Corporate segment.
- Segment results are presented on a managed (non-GAAP) basis to portray each LOB as a stand‑alone business, incorporating allocations of certain income and expenses; methodologies, assumptions, and classifications are reviewed and refined periodically.
- The Operating Committee evaluates financial information by LOB, and the firm and external stakeholders use LOB business metrics to assess performance.
- Revenue sharing: When multiple segments collaborate on client transactions, revenue is recognized in the segment owning the product/service and allocated to participating segments per agreed arrangements.
- Funds transfer pricing (FTP): The firm allocates interest income/expense to LOBs and Other Corporate and transfers primary interest rate and liquidity risk to Treasury and CIO; FTP methodologies are periodically updated to reflect economic conditions, which can affect segment net interest income.
- Foreign exchange risk for certain revenues and expenses is centralized in Treasury and CIO, which reports the impact of FX rate movements related to the transferred risk.
- Capital allocation: Equity is assigned to each LOB; assumptions and methodologies are reassessed at least annually, which may change LOB capital. As of June 30, 2023, LOB capital allocations were updated to reflect the First Republic acquisition.
- The document references additional details on managed basis, segment reporting methodology, capital allocation, and market risk management in specified pages and prior filings.
text:
Revenue sharing 
When business segments join efforts to sell products and 
services to the Firm’s clients and customers, the 
participating business segments may agree to share 
revenue from those transactions. Revenue is generally 
recognized in the segment responsible for the related 
product or service, with allocations to the other segment(s) 
involved in the transaction. The segment results reflect 
these revenue-sharing agreements.

title: Funds transfer pricing
heading: Funds transfer pricing
start_phrase: Funds transfer pricing (“FTP”) is the process by which the Firm allocates interest income and expense to the LOBs and Other Corporate and transfers the primary interest rate risk and liquidity risk to Treasury and CIO.
summary:
- Outlines the firm’s management by lines of business (LOBs): Consumer & Community Banking, Corporate & Investment Bank, Commercial Banking, Asset & Wealth Management, plus a Corporate segment.
- States segment results are presented on a managed (non-GAAP) basis aligned with how the Operating Committee evaluates performance.
- Describes the segment reporting methodology: treating each segment as a stand-alone business; allocating certain income and expenses; periodically reassessing assumptions, methodologies, and classifications; and regularly evaluating required capital for each LOB. Notes use of business metrics by management, investors, and analysts.
- Explains revenue-sharing when multiple segments collaborate, with primary revenue recognized by the product-owning segment and allocations to participating segments.
- Details funds transfer pricing (FTP) that allocates interest income/expense to LOBs and transfers primary interest rate and liquidity risks to Treasury and CIO; FTP is periodically updated and can affect net interest income allocation.
- Notes centralized management and reporting of certain foreign exchange risks by Treasury and CIO.
- Covers capital allocation to segments (equity), with at least annual reassessment; highlights updates to LOB capital allocations as of June 30, 2023, reflecting the First Republic acquisition.
- Provides references to related sections/pages in current and prior filings for definitions and further methodological detail.
text:
Funds transfer pricing (“FTP”) is the process by which the 
Firm allocates interest income and expense to the LOBs and 
Other Corporate and transfers the primary interest rate risk 
and liquidity risk to Treasury and CIO. 
The funds transfer pricing process considers the interest 
rate risk and liquidity risk characteristics of assets and 
liabilities and off-balance sheet products. Periodically the 
methodology and assumptions utilized in the FTP process 
are adjusted to reflect economic conditions and other 
factors, which may impact the allocation of net interest 
income to the segments.

title: Foreign exchange risk
heading: Foreign exchange risk
start_phrase: Foreign exchange risk is transferred from the LOBs and Other Corporate to Treasury and CIO for certain revenues and expenses.
summary:
- The firm manages and reports results by lines of business (LOBs): Consumer & Community Banking, Corporate & Investment Bank, Commercial Banking, Asset & Wealth Management, plus a Corporate segment.
- Segment results are presented on a managed basis and are intended to depict each LOB as a standalone business, including allocations of certain income and expenses; methodologies, assumptions, and classifications are periodically reassessed.
- LOBs provide business metrics used by management, investors, and analysts to assess performance.
- Revenue sharing is used when multiple LOBs collaborate on client transactions; revenue is recognized in the originating product/service segment with allocations to participating segments.
- Funds transfer pricing allocates interest income and expense to LOBs and transfers primary interest rate and liquidity risks to Treasury and CIO; FTP methodologies are updated periodically based on economic conditions.
- Certain foreign exchange risks are centralized and transferred from LOBs to Treasury and CIO, which manage and report FX impacts.
- Capital (line-of-business equity) is allocated to each LOB and reassessed at least annually; allocations were updated as of June 30, 2023, to reflect the First Republic acquisition.
- The document references additional details on managed basis definitions, methodology, and capital allocation in other sections and prior filings.
text:
Foreign exchange risk is transferred from the LOBs and 
Other Corporate to Treasury and CIO for certain revenues 
and expenses. Treasury and CIO manages these risks 
centrally and reports the impact of foreign exchange rate 
movements related to the transferred risk in its results. 
Refer to Market Risk Management on pages 84-89  for 
additional information.

title: Capital allocation
heading: Capital allocation
start_phrase: The amount of capital assigned to each business segment is referred to as equity.
summary:
- Defines the firm’s reportable segments: Consumer & Community Banking, Corporate & Investment Bank, Commercial Banking, Asset & Wealth Management, plus a Corporate segment.
- Explains that segment results are reported on a managed (non-GAAP) basis and are designed to portray each LOB as a stand-alone business.
- Describes the segment reporting methodology, including allocation of certain income and expenses, periodic reassessment of assumptions and classifications, and use of LOB business metrics.
- Outlines revenue-sharing practices when multiple segments collaborate, with primary recognition in the originating segment and allocations to others involved.
- Details funds transfer pricing (FTP), which allocates interest income/expense and transfers interest rate and liquidity risk to Treasury and CIO; methodology is updated periodically and affects net interest income allocation.
- Notes central management of foreign exchange risk by Treasury and CIO, with FX impacts reported in their results.
- Summarizes capital allocation to each LOB (equity), annual reassessment of methodologies, and updates reflecting the First Republic acquisition as of June 30, 2023.
- Provides references to related non-GAAP explanations, market risk management, and further methodological details in prior filings.
text:
Capital allocation
The amount of capital assigned to each business segment is 
referred to as equity. At least annually, the assumptions, 
judgments and methodologies  used to allocate capital are 
reassessed and, as a result, the capital allocated to the 
LOBs may change.  As of June 30, 2023, the Firm updated 
its line of business capital allocations to reflect the impact 
of the First Republic acquisition. Refer to Line of business 
equity on  page 51, and  page 93 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2022 
Form 10-K for additional information on capital allocation.
Refer to Business Segment Results – Description of business 
segment reporting methodology on pages 61-62  and Note 
32 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2022  Form 10-K for a further 
discussion of those methodologies.

title: Quarterly results
heading: Quarterly results
start_phrase: Net income was $5.3 billion , up 71% .
summary:
- Overview: Strong growth in earnings and revenue, driven primarily by higher net interest income on rising rates and increased card revolving balances, with expense and credit costs higher; First Republic acquisition boosted asset management fees and required allowance builds.

- Quarterly results:
  - Net income: $5.3B, up 71%.
  - Net revenue: $17.2B, up 37%.
  - Net interest income (NII): $13.7B, up 57%, driven by deposit margin expansion in Banking & Wealth Management (BWM) and higher NII in Card Services from increased revolving balances.
  - Noninterest revenue: $3.5B, down 8%, due to lower auto operating lease income and lower card income from increased rewards liability tied to changes in reward program terms; partially offset by higher BWM asset management fees from the First Republic acquisition.
  - Noninterest expense: $8.3B, up 9%, on higher compensation (wage inflation, headcount), marketing, and technology; partially offset by lower auto lease depreciation.
  - Provision for credit losses: $1.9B, including $1.3B net charge-offs (up $640MM, mainly Card Services as delinquencies normalize) and a $611MM net allowance build, which includes $408MM to establish allowance for First Republic loans/commitments and $203MM for Card Services (loan growth and macro outlook with U.S. unemployment peaking in 3Q24, largely offset by reduced borrower uncertainty). Prior year included a $150MM Card addition.
  - References: Notes on card income, asset management fees, MSR asset/hedges, and credit/allowance discussions.

- Year-to-date results:
  - Net income: $10.5B, up 75%.
  - Net revenue: $33.7B, up 36%.
  - NII: $26.5B, up 56%, driven by deposit margin expansion (partially offset by lower average BWM deposits) and higher Card Services NII; partially offset by lower PPP loan forgiveness in BWM.
  - Noninterest revenue: $7.2B, down 7%, due to lower auto lease income and lower Home Lending production and MSR-related net gains; partially offset by higher travel-related card commissions and higher BWM asset management fees from First Republic.
  - Card income: roughly flat; 1Q23 higher net interchange from reduced rewards costs/partner payments tied to a periodic tax refund on airline miles was offset by a 2Q23 increase to the rewards liability from reward program term changes.
  - Noninterest expense: $16.4B, up 7%, on higher compensation, marketing, and technology; partially offset by lower auto lease depreciation.
  - Provision for credit losses: $3.3B, including $2.3B net charge-offs (up $1.1B, mainly Card Services), a $553MM net allowance build (Card Services loan growth, macro outlook including unemployment peaking in 3Q24, and added weight on adverse scenarios in 1Q23; partially offset by reduced borrower uncertainty), and a $408MM addition to establish allowance for First Republic loans/commitments in 2Q23. Prior year included a $275MM addition in Card Services and Home Lending.
text:
Quarterly results 
Net income was $5.3 billion , up 71% .
Net revenue was $17.2 billion , an increase of 37% . 
Net interest income was $13.7 billion , up 57% , driven by:
•deposit margin expansion on higher rates in Banking & 
Wealth Management ("BWM"),  and
•higher NII in Card Ser vices driven by increased revolving 
balances.
Noninterest revenue was $3.5 billion , down 8%, driven by:
•lower auto operating lease income as a result of a decline 
in volume, and
•a decrease in card income driven by lower net interchange, 
as a result of an increase to t he rewards liability due to 
adjustments to certain reward program terms, 
partially offset by
•higher  asset management fees in BWM predominantly 
driven by the impact of the First Republic acquisition.

and Critical Accounting Estimates on pages 91-93  for card 
income.
Refer to Note 15 for further information regarding changes 
in the value of the MSR asset and related hedges, and 
mortgage fees and related income. 
Noninterest expense was $8.3 billion , up 9%, driven by:
•higher compensation expense, including wage inflation and 
headcount growth , as well as higher marketing  and 
technology,

title: Year-to-date results
heading: Year-to-date results
start_phrase: Net income was $10.5 billion , up 75% .
summary:
- Scope: Quarterly and year-to-date financial performance, revenue/expense drivers, credit costs, balance sheet and credit quality trends, and operating/business metrics, with multiple references to notes and clear impacts from the First Republic acquisition.

- Quarterly results:
  - Net income $5.3B, up 71%; net revenue $17.2B, up 37%.
  - Net interest income (NII) $13.7B, up 57%, driven by deposit margin expansion in Banking & Wealth Management (BWM) on higher rates and higher NII in Card Services from increased revolving balances.
  - Noninterest revenue $3.5B, down 8%, on lower auto operating lease income and reduced card income (higher rewards liability from program term adjustments), partially offset by higher asset management fees in BWM from the First Republic acquisition.
  - Noninterest expense $8.3B, up 9%, on higher compensation (wage inflation, headcount), marketing, and technology, partially offset by lower auto lease depreciation.
  - Provision for credit losses $1.9B: net charge-offs $1.3B (up $640M, mainly Card as delinquencies normalize to pre-pandemic levels) and a $611M net allowance addition, including $408M to establish the First Republic loan/commitment allowance and $203M for Card (loan growth and macro outlook with U.S. unemployment peaking in 3Q24), largely offset by reduced borrower uncertainty.

- Year-to-date results:
  - Net income $10.5B, up 75%; net revenue $33.7B, up 36%.
  - NII $26.5B, up 56% (deposit margin expansion and higher Card revolving balances), partially offset by lower PPP loan forgiveness.
  - Noninterest revenue $7.2B, down 7% (lower auto lease income; Home Lending production and lower net MSR risk management gains), partially offset by higher travel-related card commissions and higher BWM asset management fees from First Republic.
  - Card income roughly flat: Q1 benefit from reduced rewards costs and partner payments tied to a tax refund on airline miles redeemed offset by Q2 increase to the rewards liability from program term changes.
  - Noninterest expense $16.4B, up 7%, on compensation, marketing, and technology; partially offset by lower auto lease depreciation.
  - Provision $3.3B: net charge-offs $2.3B (up $1.1B, mainly Card), $553M net allowance addition (loan growth, macro, heavier adverse-scenario weighting in Q1 2023, partly offset by reduced borrower uncertainty), plus $408M allowance established for First Republic in Q2.

- Balance sheet and credit quality (selected metrics):
  - Period-end: total assets $620B (+24%), total loans $558B (+26%; strong growth in Home Lending +48%, Card +16%, Auto +8%), deposits $1.174T (flat), equity $55.5B (+11%).
  - Average deposits down 2–3%; headcount up 5%.
  - Nonaccrual loans $3.8B (−9% YoY).
  - Net charge-offs rose to $1.25B for the quarter (rate 0.98%); Card charge-offs and 30+/90+ day delinquencies increased (30+ day to 1.70% vs 1.05%).
  - Home Lending 30+ day delinquency improved (0.58% vs 0.85%).
  - Total allowance for loan losses $13.8B (+10%), including $377M tied to First Republic; adoption of updated TDR guidance on Jan 1, 2023 reduced the allowance by $591M.

- Operating and business metrics:
  - Branches 4,874 (+1%); active digital customers 65.6M (+8%); active mobile 52.0M (+10%).
  - Debit/credit card sales volume $424B (+7%); total payments volume $1.5T (flat YoY for the quarter).
  - BWM: average deposits modestly lower; deposit margin expanded to ~2.8%; client investment assets $892.9B (+42%), including ~$151B from First Republic; client advisors up 5%.
  - Home Lending: mortgage originations down sharply YoY (Q2 $11.2B, −49%); third-party servicing up; MSR carrying value up 11%.
  - Card Services: sales volume up 8–10%; net revenue rate ~9.1%; net yield on average loans ~9.3%.
  - Auto: originations up 71% in Q2; average operating lease assets down ~26–28%.

- Notable items and references:
  - Significant impacts from the First Republic acquisition across deposits, loans, client assets, and allowances.
  - Multiple references to Notes (e.g., Note 6 for card/asset management fees; Note 15 for MSR and hedges; Note 1 for TDR guidance) and to Credit/Allowance discussions for deeper detail.

summary:
- Overview of quarterly and year-to-date financial results for a financial firm, including revenue, income, expenses, credit costs, and business-line performance.
- Quarterly results:
  - Net income $4.1B, up 10%; net revenue $12.5B, up 4%.
  - Banking revenue $4.2B, up 29%.
    - Investment Banking revenue $1.5B, up 11%; excluding prior-year $257M bridge financing markdowns, down 7%.
    - Investment Banking fees down 6%; firm ranked #1 for Global IB fees (Dealogic).
      - Advisory fees $540M, down 19% amid fewer announced deals.
      - Debt underwriting fees $699M, down 6% on weaker leveraged loan issuance for acquisitions.
      - Equity underwriting fees $318M, up 30% on more convertibles and late-quarter follow-ons as equity volatility eased.
    - Payments revenue $2.5B, up 61%; excluding equity investment impacts, up 32% on deposit margin expansion despite lower average deposits.
    - Lending revenue $299M, down 27%, including $80M fair value hedge losses on retained loans.
  - Markets & Securities Services revenue $8.3B, down 5%; Markets revenue $7.0B, down 10%.
    - Fixed Income $4.6B, down 3%: lower Currencies & EM, Commodities, and Rates as volatility/activity normalized; largely offset by stronger Securitized Products and Credit Trading.
    - Equity Markets $2.5B, down 20%, mainly weaker Equity Derivatives versus a strong prior-year quarter.
    - Securities Services $1.2B, up 6% on deposit margin expansion, partly offset by lower fees and average deposits.
    - Credit Adjustments & Other gain $36M vs. prior-year loss $218M, largely driven by funding spread widening.
  - Noninterest expense $6.9B, up 1%: higher non-comp, wage inflation, and headcount; partly offset by lower revenue-related comp.
  - Provision for credit losses $38M (net charge-offs $56M) vs. $59M prior year; references to detailed credit risk and ACL sections.
- Year-to-date results:
  - Net income $8.5B, up 5%; net revenue $26.1B, up 2%.
  - Banking revenue $8.5B, up 12%.
    - Investment Banking revenue $3.1B, down 10%; excluding $257M 2Q22 bridge financing markdowns, down 17%.
    - IB fees down 13% on lower debt underwriting and advisory; firm ranked #1 for Global IB fees (Dealogic).
      - Debt underwriting $1.4B, down 22% on weaker acquisition financing issuance.
      - Advisory $1.3B, down 12% amid fewer announced deals.
      - Equity underwriting $553M, up 12% on higher convertibles and late-2Q follow-ons with lower equity volatility.
    - Payments $4.8B, up 42% on deposit margin expansion, partly offset by lower average deposits.
    - Lending $566M, down 23% due to $183M fair value hedge losses vs. $112M gains prior year; partly offset by higher net interest income.
  - Markets & Securities Services $17.7B, down 2%; Markets $15.4B, down 7%.
    - Fixed Income $10.3B, down 1%: lower Currencies & EM and Commodities; higher Rates, Securitized Products, and Credit Trading.
    - Equity Markets $5.1B, down 16%, mainly weaker Equity Derivatives.
    - Securities Services $2.4B, up 7% on deposit margin expansion, partly offset by lower fees and average deposits.
    - Credit Adjustments & Other loss $117M due to losses on certain components of FVO-elected liabilities; compared with a $742M loss in the prior year (prior-year drivers truncated in the excerpt).

Quarterly  results
Net income was $4.1 billion , up 10% .

- Scope and definitions: The Markets segment comprises Fixed Income Markets and Equity Markets. Markets revenue includes principal transactions, fees and commissions, other income, and net interest income (NII). Performance is assessed on a total revenue basis due to offsets across line items (e.g., NII on securities offset by derivatives in principal transactions). Primary source of principal transactions revenue is recognition upon execution of new transactions. References are made to Notes 6 and 7 and to the 2022 Form 10-K for line-item composition details.

- Quarterly results (three months ended June 30, 2023 vs. 2022):
  - Total Markets net revenue: $7.0B vs. $7.8B (down).
  - Noninterest revenue: $7.5B vs. $6.2B (up), driven by higher principal transactions (Fixed Income $3.1B; Equity $3.35B).
  - NII: -$0.5B vs. +$1.5B (declined), with the drop driven by higher funding costs.
  - Fixed Income total net revenue: $4.6B vs. $4.7B (slightly lower).
  - Equity total net revenue: $2.5B vs. $3.1B (lower), including negative “all other income.”

- Year-to-date results (six months ended June 30, 2023 vs. 2022):
  - Total Markets net revenue: $15.4B vs. $16.5B (down).
  - Noninterest revenue: $16.0B vs. $12.8B (up), with stronger principal transactions in both Fixed Income and Equity.
  - NII: -$0.6B vs. +$3.8B (significant decline) due to higher funding costs.
  - Fixed Income net revenue: $10.3B vs. $10.4B (flat).
  - Equity net revenue: $5.1B vs. $6.1B (down).

- Notable presentation change: Beginning Q1 2023, revenue and expense allocations to CCB associated with a Merchant Services revenue sharing agreement were discontinued and are now retained in Payments within CIB; prior periods revised accordingly.

  - Noninterest revenue $1.6B (-9%), lower deposit-related fees offset in part by higher card income.
  - Noninterest expense $2.6B (+14%), primarily higher compensation/headcount and volume-related expense.
  - Provision for credit losses $1.5B, including $608M for First Republic (Q2 2023) and $768M from a deteriorated weighted-average economic outlook, office real estate assumption updates, and net downgrade activity. Prior year provision $366M.
- References: Further detail in Credit and Investment Risk Management (pp. 62–83) and Allowance for Credit Losses (pp. 80–82).

title: Quarterly results

start_phrase: Net income was $2.6 billion , compared with a net loss of $174 million in the prior year.
summary:
- Scope: Corporate segment of JPMorgan Chase, including Treasury and CIO and Other Corporate; references to 2022 Form 10-K and various Notes for detail.
- Headline quarterly results (Q2 2023 vs Q2 2022):
  - Net income of $2.6B vs a $174M loss.
  - Total net revenue of $3.7B vs $80M, driven by higher net interest income from higher rates, partially offset by lower Firmwide average deposits available to Treasury and CIO.
  - Noninterest revenue of $2.0B vs a $244M loss, primarily:
    - Positive: $2.7B estimated bargain purchase gain from the First Republic acquisition; higher cash deployment revenue in Treasury and CIO; prior-year FX-related losses not repeating.
    - Negative: higher net investment securities losses from sales of U.S. Treasuries and agency MBS as the portfolio was repositioned; net losses on certain legacy private equity investments vs prior-year gains.
  - Noninterest expense of $1.2B, up $946M, mainly from $562M of First Republic-related expense, higher legal expense, and a larger prior-year FX benefit that did not recur.
  - Provision for credit losses: $243M net benefit from reducing the allowance tied to the Q1 2023 deposit placed with First Republic Bank.
  - Tax: expense benefited from acquisition-related tax effects embedded in the bargain purchase gain, partially offset by changes in mix of taxable income and related reserves.
- Year-to-date (1H 2023 vs 1H 2022):
  - Net income of $2.9B vs a $1.0B loss.
  - Total net revenue of $4.7B vs a $801M loss, on higher net interest income from higher rates, partly offset by lower deployable deposits in Treasury and CIO.
  - Noninterest revenue of $1.2B vs a $589M loss, with the same drivers as Q2 plus the absence of prior-year insurance settlement proceeds and lower gains on certain other Corporate investments.
  - Noninterest expense of $1.3B, up $922M, largely from First Republic-related expense, higher legal expense, and less FX-related benefit than prior year.
  - FX movements tied to risk transferred to Treasury and CIO were not material to net income.
  - Tax: benefit from acquisition-related tax effects largely offset by changes in level/mix of taxable income and related reserves.
- Segment contribution:
  - Treasury and CIO: Q2 net revenue $1.26B and net income $1.06B; 1H net revenue $2.37B and net income $1.68B.
  - Other Corporate: Q2 net revenue $2.46B and net income $1.58B; 1H net revenue $2.34B and net income $1.20B.
- Balance sheet and operational metrics (period-end vs prior year):
  - Total assets $1.264T, down 13%.
  - Loans $2.2B, roughly flat.
  - Deposits $21.1B, up 60% (predominantly from international consumer initiatives).
  - Headcount 45,235, up 12%.
- International consumer initiatives within Other Corporate: Chase U.K. (digital retail bank), Nutmeg (U.K. digital wealth manager), and 40% stake in C6 Bank (Brazil).
- Treasury and CIO investment securities portfolio:
  - Average credit rating AA+.
  - Significant investment securities losses: $900M in Q2 and $1.77B YTD, vs $153M and $547M prior-year, respectively, reflecting portfolio repositioning (sales of U.S. Treasuries and U.S. GSE/agency MBS).
  - Portfolio size (average): $609B in Q2 (down 9% YoY); period-end net $610B (down 8% YoY).
  - AFS securities period-end $201B (includes $25.8B from First Republic); HTM period-end $409B.
  - Allowance for credit losses on investment securities: $74M vs $47M prior year.
  - Accounting changes: adopted new hedge accounting guidance on Jan 1, 2023, transferring $7.1B from HTM to AFS; in 2022, $78.3B transferred from AFS to HTM for capital management.
- Notable acquisition impacts:
  - First Republic drove a $2.7B estimated bargain purchase gain, $562M of associated expenses, inclusion of AFS securities, and tax effects recorded within the bargain purchase gain.

title: FIRMWIDE RISK MANAGEMENT - Introduction
heading: 8 FIRMWIDE RISK MANAGEMENT
start_phrase: Risk is an inherent part of JPMorgan Chase’s business activities.
summary: Introduction to JPMorgan Chase’s Firmwide Risk Management outlining that risk is inherent across activities such as consumer and wholesale lending, investment advisory, market making, and other services; the objective is to manage business and associated risks to balance client, customer, and investor interests with the Firm’s safety and soundness. It specifies effective risk management principles: individual accountability for identifying and escalating risks; Lines of Business and Corporate ownership of risk identification, assessment, data, and management; and a firmwide governance and oversight structure. It also describes a disciplined, balanced compensation framework with strong internal governance and independent Board of Directors oversight, incorporating risk and control issues into performance evaluations and incentive compensation.
text:
FIRMWIDE RISK MANAGEMENT 
Risk is an inherent part of JPMorgan Chase’s business 
activities. When the Firm extends a consumer or wholesale 
loan, advises customers and clients on their investment 
decisions, makes markets in securities, or offers other 
products or services, the Firm takes on some degree of risk. 
The Firm’s overall objective is to manage its business, and 
the associated risks, in a manner that balances serving the 
interests of its clients, customers and investors, and 
protecting the safety and soundness of the Firm. 
The Firm believes that effective risk management requires, 
among other things: 
•Acceptance of responsibility, including identification and 
escalation of risks by all individuals within the Firm; 
•Ownership of risk identification, assessment, data and 
management within each of the LOBs and Corporate; and 
•A Firmwide risk governance and oversight structure. 
The Firm follows a disciplined and balanced compensation 
framework with strong internal governance and 
independent oversight by the Board of Directors (the 
“Board”). The impact of risk and control issues is carefully 
considered in the Firm’s performance evaluation and 
incentive compensation processes.

title: Basel III Overview
heading: 8.3.1 Basel III Overview
start_phrase: The capital rules under Basel III establish minimum capital ratios and overall capital adequacy standards for large and internationally active U.S. Bank Holding Companies (“BHCs” ) and banks, including the Firm and its insured depository institution (“IDI”) subsidiaries, including JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.
summary:
- Defines capital risk as the possibility that the Firm’s capital level or composition is insufficient to support activities and risks in both normal and stressed conditions, with references to the 2022 Form 10-K (pp. 86–96), this Form 10-Q Note 23, and Pillar 3 disclosures.
- Provides a Basel III overview: regulatory capital is based on risk-weighted assets (RWA) using two approaches—Standardized and Advanced—with capital adequacy assessed against the lower of the two; the Firm’s Standardized risk-based ratios are currently more binding. Notes an SLR requirement for Advanced Approaches firms and points to an SLR section for more detail.
- Details key regulatory developments:
  - CECL regulatory capital transition: the $2.9 billion COVID-related CECL capital benefit is being phased out 25% per year starting January 1, 2022; as of June 30, 2023, $1.4 billion remained in CET1. Effective January 1, 2023, 50% of other CECL transition provisions affecting Tier 2 capital, adjusted average assets, total leverage exposure, and RWA were phased out.
  - Risk-based capital targets: the Firm’s Basel III Standardized CET1 target for 1Q24 remains 13.5%, with actual quarterly ratios subject to market conditions, based on currently effective rules.
  - Basel III finalization proposal (July 2023): replaces the Advanced Approach with an expanded risk-based approach (no internal models except for market risk), applies the stress capital buffer to both expanded and standardized approaches, and significantly revises requirements for banks with assets ≥$100 billion, including U.S. GSIBs; proposed effective date July 1, 2025, with a three-year transition for the expanded approach.
  - GSIB surcharge proposal (July 2023): shifts to an annual assessment using the average of quarterly calculations (with daily averaging for certain measures), reduces surcharge increments from 50 bp to 10 bp, and includes technical Method 2 changes; would take effect two calendar quarters after the final rule.
text:
Basel III Overview
The capital rules under Basel III establish minimum capital 
ratios and overall capital adequacy standards for large and 
internationally active U.S.  Bank Holding Companies  
(“BHCs” ) and banks, including the Firm and its insured 
depository institution (“IDI”) subsidiaries,  including 
JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. The minimum amount of 
regulatory capital that must be held by BHCs and banks is 
determined by calculating risk-weighted assets ("RWA"), 
which are on-balance sheet assets and off-balance sheet 
exposures, weighted according to risk. Two comprehensive 
approaches are prescribed for calculating RWA: a 
standardized approach (“Basel III Standardized”), and an 
advanced approach (“Basel III Advanced”). For each of the 
risk-based capital ratios, the capital adequacy of the Firm is 
evaluated against the lower of the Standardized or 
Advanced approac hes compared to their respective 
regulatory capital ratio requirements.  The Firm’s Basel III 
Standardized risk-based ratios are currently more binding 
than the Basel III Advanced risk-based ratios.  
Basel III also includes a requirement for Advanced 
Approaches banking organizations, including the Firm, to 
calculate its SLR. Refer to SLR on page 51  for additional 
information.
Key Regulatory Developments

text:
In July 2023, the Federal Reserve,  the OCC and the FDIC 
released a p roposal to amend the risk-based capital 
framework, entitled "Regulatory capital rule: Amendments 
applicable to large banking organizations and to banking 
organizations with significant trading activity". Under the 
proposal, changes would include replacement of the 
advanced approach with an expanded risk-based approach, 
which would not permit the use of internal models for the 
calculation of risk-weighted assets, other than for Market 
risk. In addition, the stress capital buffer requirement would 
be applicable to both the expanded risk-based approach 
and the standardized approach. The proposal would 
significantly revise risk-based capital requirements for all 
banks with assets of $100 billion or more, including the 
Firm and other U.S. GSIBs. The proposed effective date is 
July 1, 2025 with a three year transition period applicable 
to the expanded risk -based approach.

    - Credit risk: book size changes, First Republic acquisition (including FDIC shared‑loss benefits), legacy Home Lending rolloffs, mix/credit quality shifts, market moves, and deductions for excess eligible credit reserves not includable in Tier 2.
    - Market risk: position changes, market moves, and changes in the regulatory multiplier from Regulatory VaR backtesting exceptions.
    - Operational risk: updates to cumulative losses and macroeconomic inputs.

- Transition item: Approximately $57.1bn of Credit risk RWA at June 30, 2023 calculated under the Standardized approach for certain First Republic assets per U.S. capital rules transition provisions.
- Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR): 
  - Tier 1 capital $262.6bn; total leverage exposure $4.493tn; SLR 5.8% (up from 5.6% at 12/31/22).

  - June 30, 2023 allocations: CCB $55.5bn; CIB $108.0bn; Commercial Banking $30.0bn; AWM $17.0bn; Corporate $74.6bn; total common stockholders’ equity $285.1bn (vs $275.7bn at March 31, 2023 and $264.9bn at Dec 31, 2022).

title: LCR and HQLA
heading: 8.4.1 LCR and HQLA
start_phrase: The LCR rule requires that the Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. maintain an amount of eligible HQLA that is sufficient to meet their respective estimated total net cash outflows over a prospective 30 calendar-day period of significant stress.
summary:
- Defines liquidity risk as the Firm’s potential inability to meet obligations or maintain appropriate funding and liquidity profile; points to JPMorgan Chase’s 2022 Form 10-K (pp. 97–104) and U.S. LCR Disclosure reports for more detail.
- Outlines LCR and HQLA requirements: both the Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. must maintain a minimum 100% LCR, holding sufficient eligible HQLA to cover 30 days of stressed net cash outflows. Excess HQLA at the bank that is not transferable to non-bank affiliates is excluded from the Firm’s reported HQLA.
- Provides average LCR metrics for the three months ended June 30, 2023, March 31, 2023, and June 30, 2022:
  - JPMorgan Chase & Co.: LCR 112% (Q2’23), 114% (Q1’23), 110% (Q2’22); average HQLA $768.1B (cash $440.3B; securities $327.8B); net cash outflows $683.4B; net excess eligible HQLA $84.7B. End-of-period HQLA: $791.5B (Q2’23), $758.9B (Q1’23), $721.1B (Q2’22).
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.: LCR 129% (Q2’23), 140% (Q1’23), 169% (Q2’22); net excess eligible HQLA $211.2B (Q2’23), $278.7B (Q1’23), $487.9B (Q2’22).
- Describes HQLA composition and reporting: eligible cash primarily central bank deposits; eligible securities predominantly U.S. Treasuries, U.S. GSE/agency MBS, and sovereign bonds (net of LCR haircuts); eligible HQLA securities may appear in securities financing, trading assets, or investment securities lines.
- Explains drivers of LCR changes:
  - Firm QoQ (Q2’23 vs Q1’23): lower LCR due to long-term debt maturities and capital returns (buybacks/dividends), largely offset by a dividend from the bank to the Parent Company.
  - Firm YoY (Q2’23 vs Q2’22): higher LCR driven by bank dividends to Parent, partially offset by capital returns.
  - Bank QoQ: lower LCR primarily from the First Republic acquisition (reduced HQLA and higher net cash outflows), plus lower cash due to higher average loans, a dividend to Parent, and lower average deposits.
  - Bank YoY: lower LCR due to reduced cash from deposit declines and loan growth, lower market values of HQLA-eligible securities, and the First Republic acquisition.
- Notes external influences: Federal Reserve actions have affected depositor behavior and reduced system-wide deposits, contributing to variability in LCR through changes in HQLA and estimated net cash outflows.
- Highlights internal liquidity stress testing: regular and ad hoc stress scenarios (including resolution/recovery planning) inform the funding plan and liquidity assessment; the Firm maintains adequate liquidity at the Parent Company, Intermediate Holding Company, and operating subsidiaries to meet risk tolerances and minimum requirements.
- References: additional details on HQLA and net cash outflows (2022 Form 10-K p. 98; U.S. LCR Disclosure reports) and on investment securities and the First Republic acquisition (Notes 10 and 28).
