summary:
- Scope: Presents the impact of derivatives on the Consolidated statements of income, focusing on fair value hedge accounting.
- Periods covered: Detailed results for the three and six months ended June 30, 2023 and 2022.
- Content of tables: Pre-tax gains and losses by contract type (interest rate, foreign exchange, commodity) for both the hedging derivatives and related hedged items; the Firm records derivative gains/losses in the same income statement line as the hedged item.
- Income statement and OCI effects: Breakout of (i) gains/losses recorded in income, (ii) the income statement impact of excluded hedge components (via amortization and fair value changes), and (iii) related other comprehensive income (OCI) impacts, including amounts tied predominantly to cross-currency basis spreads.
- Contract-type details:
  - Interest rate hedges primarily of benchmark (e.g., SOFR) risk on fixed-rate long-term debt and AFS securities, with effects in net interest income; includes amortization of inception hedge accounting adjustments but excludes swap interest accruals.
  - Foreign exchange hedges of spot FX risk on long-term debt and AFS securities, with impacts primarily in principal transactions revenue and net interest income.
  - Commodity hedges of physical inventory positions (overall fair value hedges), with impacts in principal transactions revenue.
- Hedge effectiveness exclusions: Forward points, time value, and cross-currency basis spreads are excluded from effectiveness testing and recognized either via amortization over the derivative’s life or current-period fair value changes; related OCI reflects changes in excluded amounts under the amortization approach.
- Balance sheet basis adjustments: Discloses cumulative fair value hedge basis adjustments embedded in AFS investment securities and long-term debt at June 30, 2023 and December 31, 2022, split between active and discontinued hedging relationships; notes these amounts will reverse through income as yield adjustments, with sign conventions indicating direction of future net interest income effects.
- Portfolio layer method: Notes adoption effective January 1, 2023, expanding hedging of portfolios of prepayable assets; provides amounts for closed portfolios designated as hedged and the associated cumulative basis adjustments for active and discontinued hedges.
- Exclusions and clarifications: 
  - Physical commodities inventories under fair value hedge accounting are carried at fair value, so unrealized gains/losses are recognized currently with no incremental future net income impact upon exit.
  - Hedged items where only FX risk is designated are excluded from basis adjustments expected to reverse through the income statement; amounts excluded for AFS securities and long-term debt are disclosed.

summary:
- Scope and references: Note 6 focuses on noninterest revenue (noninterest expense not detailed in this excerpt). It references the Firm’s 2022 Form 10-K for accounting policies, Note 7 for interest income/expense on trading positions, and Note 28 for impacts of the First Republic acquisition.
- Investment banking fees: Reported by underwriting (equity and debt) and advisory. Q2 2023 total $1,513mm vs $1,586mm in Q2 2022; 1H 2023 $3,162mm vs $3,594mm. Underwriting improved year-over-year in Q2 (equity higher, debt roughly flat/lower), while advisory declined.
- Principal transactions: Presents realized and unrealized gains/losses; excludes interest income/expense on trading assets/liabilities. Trading revenue is shown by instrument (interest rate, credit, FX, equity, commodity) and is not indicative of any single line-of-business total. Q2 2023 trading revenue $6,944mm vs $4,882mm; 1H 2023 $14,534mm vs $10,134mm, with notable strength in interest rate and equity. Private equity results: Q2 2023 loss of $34mm vs gain of $108mm; 1H 2023 loss of $9mm vs loss of $39mm. Total principal transactions: Q2 2023 $6,910mm vs $4,990mm; 1H 2023 $14,525mm vs $10,095mm. Footnotes note inclusion of FVA (interest rate) and CVA net of hedges (credit), and prior markdowns on held-for-sale bridge financing positions.

text:
FDIC Special Assessment
In May 2023, the FDIC issued a notice of proposed 
rulemaking recommending a special assessment  related to 
the systemic risk determination made on March 12, 2023, 
to recover losses to the Deposit Insurance Fund ("DIF") 
arising from the protection of uninsured depositors 
resulting from recent bank resolutions. In its current form, 
the rule would impose a special assessment at an annual 
rate of 12.5 basis points on certain banks’ estimated 
uninsured deposits reported as of December 31, 2022.  The 
Firm expects to be subject to special assessments imposed 
by the FDIC to recover losses to the DIF.

start_phrase: The following table presents the amortized cost and estimated fair valu e at J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 3, of JPMorgan Chase ’s invest ment securities portfolio by contractual maturity.
summary:
- Presents JPMorgan Chase’s investment securities portfolio by contractual maturity as of June 30, 2023, split between available-for-sale (AFS) and held-to-maturity (HTM), with amortized cost, estimated fair value, and average yields for each maturity bucket and security type.
- AFS securities:
  - Total amortized cost $210.8 billion; fair value $203.3 billion; total average yield 4.63%.
  - Major categories: mortgage-backed securities (MBS) $90.6B amortized cost (fair value $85.4B), U.S. Treasury and agencies $64.0B, obligations of U.S. states and municipalities $24.3B, non-U.S. government debt $22.6B, asset-backed $8.8B, corporate $0.4B.
  - Notes: AFS includes securities from the First Republic acquisition, primarily in the >10-year bucket; AFS amortized cost excludes $30 million allowance for credit losses and $(865) million portfolio layer hedge basis adjustments.
- HTM securities:
  - Total amortized cost $409.0 billion; fair value $375.3 billion; total average yield 2.42%.
  - Major categories: U.S. Treasury and agencies $202.7B, MBS $131.6B, asset-backed $63.1B, obligations of U.S. states and municipalities $11.7B.
  - HTM amortized cost excludes $74 million allowance for credit losses.
- Yield methodology and maturity considerations:
  - Average yields are effective yields weighted by amortized cost, reflecting coupons, premium/discount amortization, and related hedging (including closed portfolio hedges); taxable-equivalent where applicable.
  - Excludes unscheduled prepayments; certain callable debt yields are to earliest call date.
  - Substantially all U.S. residential MBS/CMOs are contractually due after 10 years; estimated weighted-average lives reflect prepayments (about 8 years for agency residential MBS, 7 for agency residential CMOs, 6 for nonagency residential CMOs).
- Securities financing activities (Note 11):
  - Summarizes gross and net amounts for securities financing agreements (reverse repos, securities borrowed, repos, and securities loaned) as of June 30, 2023 and December 31, 2022.
  - Explains balance sheet netting under U.S. GAAP when master netting agreements and appropriate legal opinions exist; collateral exchanged reduces economic exposure but is not eligible for balance sheet netting and is shown as “Amounts not nettable.”

Transfers not qualifying for sale accounting
At both J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 3, and D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  2 0 2 2, the Firm held $692 million  of financial assets for which the rights have been 
transferred to third parties; however, the  transfers did not qualify as a sale in accordance with U.S. GAAP. These transfers have 
been recognized as collateralized financing transactions. The transfer red assets are recorded in trading assets and loans, and 
the corresponding liabilities are recorded predominantly in short-term borrowings on the Consolidated balance sheets.

title: Loan accounting framework
heading: Loan accounting framework
start_phrase: The accounting for a loan depends on management’s strategy for the loan.
summary:
- Overview: Note 12 outlines JPMorgan Chase’s loan accounting framework, portfolio segmentation, the impact of new credit loss disclosure guidance adopted in 2023, and a snapshot of loan balances as of June 30, 2023 versus December 31, 2022.
- Loan accounting framework: Loans are categorized as (1) originated or purchased loans held-for-investment (retained), (2) loans held-for-sale, and (3) loans at fair value. The note cross-references the 2022 Form 10-K (loan policies), and this Form 10-Q’s Notes 2 (trading assets at fair value) and 3 (fair value option elections).
- New guidance adoption (effective Jan 1, 2023): The Firm adopted Financial Instruments—Credit Losses guidance eliminating Troubled Debt Restructuring (TDR) accounting/disclosures and adding disclosure requirements for FDMs, including current-period gross charge-offs by vintage origination year. Pre-2023 TDR discussion is referenced to the 2022 Form 10-K.
- Portfolio structure: The loan portfolio is grouped into three segments aligned with allowance methodology—Consumer excluding credit card; Credit card; and Wholesale. Classes within segments include residential real estate; auto and other (consumer); credit card loans; and wholesale classes secured by real estate, commercial and industrial, and other. Wholesale classes align with regulatory loan classifications. “Other” includes loans to financial institutions, governments, SPEs, nonprofits, personal investment companies, trusts, and individuals across multiple business lines (CIB, CB, AWM, CCB).
- First Republic acquisition: The portfolio includes $149.8 billion of loans from the acquisition—$91.9 billion retained and $1.9 billion at fair value in Consumer (excluding credit card), and $56.0 billion retained in Wholesale.
- Loan balances:
  - June 30, 2023: Total loans $1,300.1 billion, comprising Retained $1,255.7 billion, Held-for-sale $5.6 billion, and At fair value $38.8 billion. By segment: Consumer excluding credit card $408.2 billion; Credit card $191.3 billion; Wholesale $700.5 billion.
  - December 31, 2022: Total loans $1,135.6 billion, comprising Retained $1,089.6 billion, Held-for-sale $4.0 billion, and At fair value $42.1 billion. By segment: Consumer excluding credit card $311.4 billion; Credit card $185.2 billion; Wholesale $639.1 billion.
- Presentation notes: Accrued interest receivables of $6.0 billion (June 30, 2023) and $5.2 billion (December 31, 2022) are excluded; write-offs of accrued interest were not material. Amounts are presented net of unamortized discounts/premiums and net deferred fees/costs (not material).
text:
Loan accounting framework
The accounting for a loan depends on management’s strategy for the loan.  The Firm accounts for loans based on the following 
categories:
•Originated or purchased loans held-for-investment (i.e., “retained”)
•Loans held-for-sale
•Loans at fair value
Refer to Note  12 of JPMorgan Chase's 2022 Form 10-K for a detailed discussion of loans, including accounting policies. Refer 
to Note  3 of this Form 10-Q for further information on  the Firm's elections of fair value accounting under the fair value option. 
Refer to Note  2 of this Form 10-Q for information on loans carried at fair value and classified as trading assets.  
On January 1, 2023  the Firm adopted the Financial Instruments - Credit Losses: Troubled Debt Restructurings and Vintage 
Disclosures accounting guidance as discussed in Note  1. The adoption of this guidance eliminated the existing accounting and 
disclosure requirements for TDRs, and implemented additional disclosure requirements for FDMs. The disclosure requirements 
for FDMs are effective for periods beginning on or after  January 1, 2023. Refer to Note  12 of JPMorgan Chase's 2022 Form 
10-K for a detailed discussion on loan modifications prior to  January 1, 2023 , which were accounted for and reported as TDRs. 
This new guidance also requires disclosure of current period gross charge-offs by vintage origination year, effective for periods 
beginning on or after  January 1, 2023.

start_phrase: Net gains/(losses) on sales of loans and lending-related commitments (including adjustments to record loans and lending- related commitments held-for-sale at the lower of cost or fair value) recognized in noninterest revenue for the three and six months ended J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 3,
summary:
- Scope: Tables summarize carrying value activity for retained loans purchased, sold, and reclassified to held-for-sale (HFS) for the three and six months ended June 30, 2023 and 2022, by portfolio: Consumer (excluding credit card), Credit card, and Wholesale. Loans first reclassified to HFS and sold later are excluded from the sales line.
- Three months ended June 30:
  - 2023 purchases: $150.4B total ($92.002B Consumer ex-CC; $58.398B Wholesale; $0 Credit card).
  - 2023 sales: $10.147B total ($438M Consumer ex-CC; $9.709B Wholesale; $0 Credit card).
  - 2023 reclassified to HFS (non-cash): $852M total ($81M Consumer ex-CC; $771M Wholesale; $0 Credit card).
  - 2022 purchases: $1.201B total; sales: $12.087B; reclassified to HFS: $481M.
- Six months ended June 30:
  - 2023 purchases: $150.642B total ($92.081B Consumer ex-CC; $58.561B Wholesale; $0 Credit card).
  - 2023 sales: $19.318B total ($438M Consumer ex-CC; $18.880B Wholesale; $0 Credit card).
  - 2023 reclassified to HFS (non-cash): $1.209B total ($124M Consumer ex-CC; $1.085B Wholesale; $0 Credit card).
  - 2022 purchases: $1.486B total; sales: $21.841B; reclassified to HFS: $830M.
- First Republic acquisition impact: Purchases include loans acquired in 2023 totaling $91.9B in Consumer (excluding credit card) and $58.4B in Wholesale.
- Additional purchase details:
  - Includes purchases of residential real estate loans, including voluntary repurchases of certain delinquent Ginnie Mae pool loans, with ongoing servicing/foreclosure management per Ginnie Mae, FHA, RHS, and VA guidelines.
  - Excludes certain purchases of retained loans sourced mainly through the correspondent channel and underwritten to firm standards: $1.6B (3Q23 YTD quarter), $6.0B (3Q22 quarter), $2.3B (6M23), and $9.2B (6M22).
- Gains and losses:
  - 2023: Net gains on sales of loans and lending-related commitments recognized in noninterest revenue were $14M (three months) and $37M (six months), of which $16M and $43M, respectively, related to loans.
  - 2022: Net losses were $(352)M (three months) and $(314)M (six months), of which $(67)M and $(32)M, respectively, related to loans.
  - Note: Loan sales can also lead to write-downs, recoveries, or allowance changes recorded in the provision for credit losses.

title: Residential real estate
heading: Residential real estate
start_phrase: Delinquency is the primary credit quality indicator for retained residential real estate loans.
summary:
- Focus: Credit quality of retained residential real estate loans, using delinquency as the primary indicator. Tables present delinquency and gross charge-offs for the six months ended June 30, 2023, with a comparison to December 31, 2022.
- Portfolio size and status:
  - Total retained loans: $328.0 billion at June 30, 2023 vs. $237.6 billion at December 31, 2022.
  - At June 30, 2023: current $326.2 billion; 30–149 days past due $1.101 billion; 150+ days past due $0.676 billion.
- Delinquency rates (30+ days past due to total):
  - Overall: 0.54% at June 30, 2023 vs. 0.66% at December 31, 2022.
  - By segment (June 30, 2023 examples): Prior to 2019 term loans 1.75%; converted revolving loans 4.23% (higher than revolving within period), reflecting higher fully amortizing payments after conversion; recent vintages (2019–2023) exhibit very low delinquency rates (generally below ~0.25%).
- Product/vintage segmentation:
  - Term loans shown by origination year; revolving loans split between within the revolving period and converted to term loans.
  - Converted revolving loans have higher delinquency than revolving loans still within the revolving period due to payment structure differences.
- Gross charge-offs (six months ended June 30, 2023): $70 million total, concentrated in older vintages and revolving products ($52 million in prior-to-2019 term loans; $14 million in revolving within period; $4 million in converted revolving).
- First Republic acquisition impact:
  - Included across vintages: $5.6b (2023), $26.2b (2022), $22.0b (2021), $15.0b (2020), $7.5b (2019), $12.9b (prior to 2019) in term loans; $2.5b in revolving within the period.
  - $158 million of 30+ days past due loans are associated with the acquisition.
- Methodology/footnotes:
  - Government-insured mortgage loans were not material; 30+ day delinquency ratios exclude such loans due to the guarantee.
  - Loans in COVID-19 deferral programs, performing under modified terms within the deferral period, are generally not considered delinquent.
  - Purchased loans are reported by their original origination year.
  - Approximately 37% of revolving loans are senior liens; lien position is considered in the allowance for credit losses.

title: Nonaccrual loans and other credit quality indicators
heading: Nonaccrual loans and other credit quality indicators
start_phrase: The following table provides information on nonaccrual and other credit quality indicators for retained residential real estate loans.
summary:
- Presents nonaccrual and credit quality metrics for retained residential real estate loans as of June 30, 2023 versus December 31, 2022.
- Nonaccrual loans were $3.641 billion (vs. $3.745 billion).
- Total retained loans rose to $328.0 billion (vs. $237.6 billion), including $91.9 billion from the First Republic acquisition.
- Credit quality mix by current estimated LTV and refreshed FICO shows:
  - Portfolio concentrated in low LTV, high FICO: <$80% LTV and FICO ≥660 totaled $298.8 billion in 2023.
  - Smaller balances at higher LTVs and/or lower FICOs; $1.526 billion had no FICO/LTV available.
- Weighted-average metrics were stable: LTV 51% and FICO 771 (vs. 51% and 769).
- Geographic concentrations highlight largest exposures in California ($128.0 billion), New York ($49.4 billion), Florida ($22.5 billion), Texas ($15.4 billion), and Massachusetts ($14.4 billion), with significant increases tied to First Republic (e.g., +$55.5B CA, +$15.2B NY, +$3.6B FL, +$8.0B MA).
- Footnotes summarize methodology and policies:
  - Nonaccrual includes collateral-dependent and Chapter 7 discharged loans (about 9% of Chapter 7 loans were 30+ days past due at June 30, 2023); government-insured loans excluded from nonaccrual were immaterial.
  - Consumer nonaccrual loans generally carry allowances; collateral-dependent loans may be charged down; allowance can be negative if collateral values later improve.
  - Interest income on nonaccrual loans recognized on a cash basis was $44 million for Q2 2023 and $89 million year-to-date (comparatives provided for 2022).
  - Loans under COVID-19 deferral programs are generally excluded.
  - LTVs are based on model-estimated current property values; refreshed FICOs are updated at least quarterly; some loans without refreshed FICO were bucketed by management estimate.
  - Weighted averages exclude loans with missing FICO/LTV; prior-period amounts were revised to conform to current presentation.

title: Loan modifications
heading: Loan modifications
start_phrase: The Firm grants certain modifications of residential real estate loans to borrowers experiencing financial difficulty, which effective January 1, 2023, are reported as FDMs.
summary:
- Shift in accounting for residential real estate loan modifications effective January 1, 2023: modifications for borrowers experiencing financial difficulty are reported as FDMs, replacing prior TDR accounting. FDMs include proprietary and U.S. GSE programs offering interest rate reductions, term extensions, other-than-insignificant payment delays, and principal forgiveness.
- 2023 activity and effects (three and six months ended June 30, 2023): $35 million and $75 million of FDMs; primarily term extensions and interest rate reductions that extended weighted-average loan life by 15 and 18 years and reduced weighted-average contractual rates from 6.90% to 4.21% and 6.75% to 4.01%, respectively; no additional lending commitments to FDM borrowers. Also reported: $33 million/$48 million of loans in trial modification and $3 million/$5 million of Chapter 7 loans—considered TDRs but not FDMs under revised guidance.
- Pre-2023 (TDR framework): For the three and six months ended June 30, 2022, new TDRs were $115 million and $233 million; no additional lending commitments to TDR borrowers; reference to the firm’s 2022 Form 10-K for more TDR information.
- Nature and extent of 2022 TDR modifications: 1,165/2,691 loans approved for trial modification and 1,289/2,831 permanently modified (three/six months). Concessions on permanent mods (percent of loans; multiple concessions common): interest rate reductions 45%/56%; term/payment extensions 54%/67%; principal/interest deferred 10%/12%; principal forgiveness 1%/1%; other (e.g., variable-to-fixed, qualifying payment delays) 46%/36%.
- Financial effects and redefaults for 2022 TDRs: Weighted-average interest rate reduced from 4.76% to 3.36% (three months) and 4.55% to 3.31% (six months). Remaining contractual term extended from 22 to 38 years and 23 to 39 years. Charge-offs on permanent mods $1 million/$1 million; principal deferred $4 million/$11 million; principal forgiven $0/$1 million. Redefault balances within one year of permanent modification were $27 million/$70 million.
text:
Loan modifications
The Firm grants certain modifications of residential real 
estate loans to borrowers experiencing financial difficulty, 
which effective January 1, 2023, are reported as FDMs.  The 
Firm's proprietary modification programs as well as 
government programs, including U.S. GSE programs, that 
generally provide variou s modifications to borrowers 
experiencing financial difficulty including, but not limited 
to, interest rate reductions, term extensions, other-than-
insignificant payment delay and principal forgiveness that 
would otherwise have been required under the terms of the 
original agreement, are considered FDMs.  
For the  three and six months ended  J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 3, 
residential real estate FDMs were  $35 million  and $75 
million , respectively. The financial effects of the FDMs, 
which were largely in the form of term extensions and 
interest rate reductions, included extending the weighted-
average life of the loans by  15 years  and 18 years , and 
reducing the weighted-average contractual interest rate 
from  6.90%  to 4.21%  and 6.75%  to 4.01%  for the three 
and six months ended June 30, 2023, respectively.  There 
were  no additional commitments  to lend to borrowers 
experiencing financial difficulty whose loans have been 
modified as FDMs. In addition to FDMs,  the Firm also had  
$ 3 3  m i l l i o n and $ 4 8  m i l l i o n of loans subject to a trial 
modification , and $ 3  m i l l i o n and $ 5  m i l l i o n of Chapter 7 
loans for the  three and six months ended  J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 3, 
respectively. The changes to the TDR accounting guidance 
eliminated the TDR reasonably expected and concession 
assessment criteria. Accordingly, trial modifications and 
Chapter 7 loans were considered TDRs, but not FDMs.

title: Loan modifications
heading: Loan modifications
start_phrase: The Firm grants certain modifications of credit card loans to borrowers experiencing financial difficulty, which effective January 1, 2023, are reported as FDMs.
summary:
- Overview: The firm modifies credit card loans for borrowers experiencing financial difficulty. Effective January 1, 2023, these are reported as Financial Difficulty Modifications (FDMs), replacing prior TDR accounting.
- Nature of modifications: Customers are placed on fixed payment plans (generally 60 months) with substantial interest rate reductions; credit lines are generally not reinstated. Noncompliance results in continued aging and eventual charge-off under standard policy.
- Volume and terms (2023):
  - Three months ended June 30, 2023: $181 million of FDMs (0.09% of total retained credit card loans); weighted-average contractual interest rate reduced from 23.27% to 3.57%.
  - Six months ended June 30, 2023: $326 million (0.17%); rate reduced from 22.96% to 3.54%.
  - Interest rates are weighted averages at enrollment; term extensions reflect placement on fixed payment plans.
- Trial modifications: $26 million of loans were subject to trial modifications in both the three- and six-month periods; due to changes eliminating certain TDR criteria, trial mods are not considered FDMs.
- Payment status of FDMs (amortized cost basis):
  - Three months ended June 30, 2023: $128m current/<30 DPD; $32m 30–89 DPD; $21m 90+ DPD; total $181m.
  - Six months ended June 30, 2023: $264m current/<30 DPD; $38m 30–89 DPD; $24m 90+ DPD; total $326m.
- Redefaults and default policy: $6 million of FDMs redefaulted in both the three- and six-month periods. Payment default is defined as two consecutive missed payments; defaulted loans remain in the program and are charged off per standard policy.
- Prior-period (2022) TDR comparison: New TDR enrollments were less than 1% of total retained credit card loans; balances of new TDRs were $81m (Q2) and $163m (H1). Weighted-average interest rates declined from 18.94%/18.47% pre-TDR to 4.62%/4.75% post-TDR. Redefaults within one year were $8m (Q2) and $17m (H1).
text:
Loan modifications
The Firm grants certain modifications of credit card loans to borrowers experiencing financial difficulty, which effective January 
1, 2023, are reported as FDMs. These modifications involve placing the customer on a fixed payment plan, generally for  60 
months , and typically include reducing the interest rate on the credit card under long-term programs. If the cardholder does not 
comply with the modified payment terms, then the credit card loan continues to age and will ultimately be charged-off in 
accordance with  the Firm's standard charge-off policy. In most cases,  the Firm does not reinstate the borrower's line of credit.

heading: Loan modifications
start_phrase: The Firm grants certain modifications of wholesale loans to borrowers experiencing financial difficulty, which effective January 1, 2023, are reported as FDMs.
summary:
- Overview: The firm discloses loan modifications for borrowers experiencing financial difficulty (FDMs), effective January 1, 2023. FDMs replace prior TDR disclosures, with a broader population due to removal of the “concession” assessment. Comparative 2022 TDR amounts are provided.

- Commercial and industrial (C&I) FDMs:
  - Q2 2023: $312 million; YTD 2023: $469 million. Small share of total C&I loans (around 0.18%–0.25% for key categories).
  - Predominantly term extensions (Q2: $306m, avg +8 months; YTD: $423m, avg +10 months).
  - Other modifications include payment deferrals re-amortized ($5m), combined interest rate reductions and term extensions (rate down ~191 bps; minimal balances), and YTD principal forgiveness with term extension ($40m; avg +64 months; $23m write-down).
  - Payment status: Majority current or <30 days past due (Q2: $242m; YTD: $331m); small 90+ days past due ($3m); criticized nonaccrual increased (Q2: $67m; YTD: $135m).
  - Re-defaults (30+ days past due): limited to term extensions ($3m in Q2; $7m YTD).
  - Additional lending commitments to these borrowers: $438 million in Q2; $1.3 billion YTD.

- Other loans FDMs:
  - Q2 2023: $284 million; YTD 2023: $300 million.
  - Dominated by combined payment deferral and term extension ($235m; avg +144 months; deferrals recaptured at end of period).
  - Smaller items: interest rate reductions ($11m; ~654 bps) and short term extensions (Q2: $38m, +3 months; YTD: $54m, +6 months).
  - Payment status: Entire balance categorized as criticized nonaccrual; no current or past-due-accruing amounts.
  - Re-defaults: none.
  - Additional lending commitments: none.

- Secured by real estate FDMs:
  - Q2 2023: $77 million; YTD 2023: $85 million.
  - Largely term extensions (avg +9 months).
  - Re-defaults: none in Q2; $1 million YTD.
  - No additional lending commitments.

- Prior TDR context (pre-2023):
  - New TDRs in Q2 2022: $60 million; YTD 2022: $479 million, mainly maturity extensions and covenant waivers in C&I; impacts not material.

title: Allowance for credit losses - Introduction
heading: Note 13 – Allowance for credit losses
start_phrase: The Firm's allowance for credit losses represe nts management's estimate of expected credit losses over the remaining expected life of the Firm's financial assets measured at amortized cost and certain off-balance sheet lending-related commitments.
summary: Introduces JPMorgan Chase’s allowance for credit losses (ACL) as management’s estimate of expected losses over the remaining life of financial assets at amortized cost and certain off-balance sheet lending commitments, and notes adoption on January 1, 2023 of the Financial Instruments – Credit Losses: Troubled Debt Restructurings guidance (see Note 1). The new guidance removes the requirement to use a DCF approach for TDRs, permits a non-DCF portfolio-based method for modified loans to borrowers in financial difficulty, and, if DCF is used, requires the post-modification effective interest rate. The Firm elected a non-DCF, portfolio-based allowance for such modified loans across portfolios, except for collateral-dependent loans and nonaccrual risk-rated loans which remain asset-specific. Adopted via the modified retrospective method, the change decreased the ACL by $587 million and increased retained earnings by $446 million after-tax, largely driven by residential real estate and credit card; see 2022 Form 10-K Note 13 for detailed policies.
text:
Allowance for credit losses
The Firm's allowance for credit losses represe nts 
management's estimate of expected credit losses over the 
remaining expected life of the  Firm's financial assets 
measured at amortized cost and certain off-balance sheet 
lending-related commitments.
On January 1, 2023  the Firm adopted the Financial 
Instruments - Credit Losses: Troubled Debt Restructurings 
accounting guidance as described in Note  1.
The adoption of this guidance eliminated the requirement 
to measure the allowance for TDRs using a DCF 
methodology and allowed the option of a non-DCF portfolio-
based approach for modified loans to borrowers 
experiencing financial difficulty. If a DCF methodology is 
still applied for these modified loans, the discount rate must 
be the post-modification effective interest rate, instead of 
the pre-modification effective interest rate.  
The Firm elected to change from an asset-specific allowance 
approach to its non-DCF, portfolio-based allowance 
approach for modified loans to troubled borrowers for all 
portfolios except collateral-dependent loans and nonaccrual 
risk-rated loans, for which the asset-specific allowance 
approach will continue to apply.
This guidance was adopted under the modified 
retrospective method which resulted in a net decrease to 
the allowance for credit losses of  $ 5 8 7  m i l l i o n and an 
increase to retained earnings of  $ 4 4 6  m i l l i o n, after-tax 
predominantly driven by residential real estate and credit 
card.
Refer to Note  13 of JPMorgan Chase's 2022  Form 10-K  for 
a detailed discussion of the allowance for credit losses and 
the related accounting policies.
162

  - Allowance for loan losses increased to $21.98B (from $17.75B); allowance for lending-related commitments slightly decreased to $2.19B (from $2.22B); allowance for investment securities increased to $104M (from $47M).

  - Cumulative effect of new TDR accounting reduced allowance by $587M in 1H23.
  - Net charge-offs rose to $2.55B (from $1.24B), driven primarily by Credit card and Wholesale.
  - Provision expense increased to $5.36B (from $2.60B), with larger builds in Credit card and Wholesale.
  - Ending balance: $21.98B (vs $17.75B).

title: Discussion of changes in the allowance
heading: Discussion of changes in the allowance
start_phrase: The allowance for credit losses as of J u n e 3 0 , 2 0 2 3 was $24.3 billion , reflecting a net additio n of $2.7 billion from D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 2.
summary:
- Allowance for credit losses (ACL) stood at $24.3 billion as of June 30, 2023, a net increase of $2.7 billion from December 31, 2022.
- Drivers of the net addition:
  - $1.5 billion reserve build:
    - $819 million in wholesale, driven by net downgrade activity, revised office real estate assumptions in Commercial Banking in 2Q23, and higher weighting of adverse scenarios initiated in 1Q23.
    - $649 million in consumer, largely in Card Services, reflecting loan growth and macro outlook changes (including weighted-average U.S. unemployment peaking in 3Q24), and higher adverse scenario weighting in 1Q23, partially offset by reduced borrower uncertainty.
  - $1.2 billion established for First Republic loans and lending-related commitments in 2Q23.
  - Partially offset by a $587 million reduction from adopting updated TDR accounting guidance on January 1, 2023.
- Scenario methodology and outlook:
  - ACL estimated using a weighted average of five internal macroeconomic scenarios; the Firm maintained higher weight on adverse scenarios from 1Q23 due to tighter financial conditions and increased recession probability.
  - Adverse scenarios imply a weighted-average U.S. unemployment peak of 5.8% in 3Q24 and U.S. real GDP 1.5% lower by end-4Q24.
  - Central case assumptions at June 30, 2023: U.S. unemployment 4.2% (4Q23), 4.9% (2Q24), 5.0% (4Q24); YoY real GDP growth 0.5%, 0.0%, 1.0%. December 31, 2022 central case for comparison: unemployment 3.8% (2Q23), 4.3% (4Q23), 5.0% (2Q24); GDP 1.5%, 0.4%, 0.0%.
  - Future updates to forecasts will be reflected in provisions for credit losses.
- Cross-references provided to 2022 Form 10-K notes and sections for ACL policies, consumer and wholesale credit portfolios, and critical accounting estimates.
- Variable Interest Entities (Note 14):
  - Defines “Firm-sponsored” VIEs and summarizes significant types by business segment.
  - Key structures:
    - CCB: credit card securitization trusts; mortgage securitization trusts (servicing and securitization of originated/purchased residential mortgages).
    - CIB: mortgage and other securitization trusts (residential, commercial, other consumer loans); multi-seller conduits; municipal bond vehicles.
  - The Firm is the primary beneficiary of the Chase Issuance Trust due to continuing involvement.
  - The Firm may act as servicer and/or retain beneficial interests in mortgage and other securitization trusts.
  - The Firm also invests in and provides financing/services to third-party-sponsored VIEs; references to pages 165–169 for consolidated VIE assets/liabilities and additional details.

title: Firm-sponsored mortgage and other securitization trusts
heading: Firm-sponsored mortgage and other securitization trusts
start_phrase: The Firm securitizes (or has securitized) originated and purchased residential mortgages, commercial mortgages and other consumer loans primarily in its CCB and CIB businesses.
summary:
- Scope and references: Note 14 summarizes JPMorgan Chase’s involvement with variable interest entities (VIEs), referring to the Firm’s 2022 Form 10-K (Notes 1 and 14) for accounting policies and additional detail.
- Definition of Firm-sponsored VIEs: Includes entities where (1) JPMorgan Chase is the primary beneficiary; (2) the VIE is used to securitize Firm assets; (3) the VIE issues instruments bearing the JPMorgan Chase name; or (4) the entity is a JPMorgan Chase–administered asset-backed commercial paper conduit.
- Types of Firm-sponsored VIEs by business segment:
  - CCB: Credit card securitization trusts; mortgage securitization trusts (servicing and securitization of originated and purchased residential mortgages).
  - CIB: Mortgage and other securitization trusts (residential and commercial mortgages and other consumer loans); multi-seller conduits (client financing/market access and transaction structuring); municipal bond vehicles (financing municipal bond investments).
- Third-party VIEs: The Firm also invests in, finances, and provides services to VIEs sponsored by third parties; additional details on consolidated VIE assets/liabilities and third-party VIEs are referenced.
- Significant Firm-sponsored VIEs:
  - Credit card securitizations: Due to continuing involvement, the Firm is the primary beneficiary of the Chase Issuance Trust.
  - Mortgage and other securitization trusts: The Firm securitizes originated and purchased residential and commercial mortgages and other consumer loans (primarily in CCB and CIB), may act as servicer, and may retain beneficial interests.
- Continuing involvement and risk:
  - Continuing involvement may include servicing, holding senior/subordinated interests (including required risk-retention), recourse/guarantee arrangements, and derivative contracts; sometimes involvement is limited to servicing.
  - The Firm’s maximum loss exposure from retained and purchased interests equals the carrying value of those interests.
- Quantitative overview of Firm-sponsored private-label securitizations (excludes GSE/government agency securitizations):
  - June 30, 2023: Total assets held by securitization VIEs ≈ $228.7B; consolidated VIE assets ≈ $0.7B; nonconsolidated VIE assets with continuing involvement ≈ $167.6B. JPMorgan Chase interests in nonconsolidated VIEs total ≈ $9.8B (trading ≈ $1.6B; investment securities ≈ $7.5B; other financial assets ≈ $0.7B), spanning prime/Alt-A residential, subprime residential, and commercial/other pools.
  - December 31, 2022: Total assets held by securitization VIEs ≈ $230.0B; consolidated ≈ $0.8B; nonconsolidated with continuing involvement ≈ $165.8B. JPMorgan Chase interests total ≈ $9.6B (trading ≈ $1.6B; investment securities ≈ $7.3B; other financial assets ≈ $0.7B).
- Footnote highlights:
  - “Commercial and other” includes securities backed by commercial real estate loans and non-mortgage consumer receivables.
  - Exclusions from reported interests include retained servicing, GSE/government-related retained securities, certain risk-management derivatives, and select secondary market-making positions.
  - Interests include re-securitizations.
  - Credit quality: As of both June 30, 2023, and December 31, 2022, 84% of retained securitization interests (predominantly at fair value and including risk-retention amounts) were rated A or better (S&P-equivalent). Prime residential retained interests were roughly $2.7B (2023) and $2.6B (2022), with noninvestment-grade amounts not material; commercial/other retained interests included about $5.9B (2023) and $5.8B (2022) investment-grade and $1.1B noninvestment-grade at both dates.

summary:
- Focus: Summary of JPMorgan Chase’s consolidated variable interest entity (VIE) assets and liabilities, plus disclosures on involvement with third‑party VIEs and unconsolidated tax credit vehicles.
- Consolidated VIE balances:

  - December 31, 2022: Total assets $37.1B; total liabilities $12.9B (beneficial interests $12.6B; other $0.28B).
  - Largest program: Firm‑administered multi‑seller conduits (assets $28.8B; liabilities $16.4B at 6/30/23), followed by firm‑sponsored credit card trusts (assets $9.3B; liabilities $1.0B).

- Composition notes:
  - Asset categories include trading assets, loans, and “other” (cash and other assets).
  - Liabilities split between “beneficial interests in VIE assets” and “other” (accounts payable and other liabilities).
  - Assets of consolidated VIEs are used to settle their own liabilities and include third‑party positions; intercompany amounts are eliminated.
  - Beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs are recorded in a dedicated balance sheet line; holders generally have no recourse to JPMorgan Chase.
  - Long‑term beneficial interests outstanding: $1.1B at 6/30/23 vs. $2.1B at 12/31/22.
  - “Other” assets category primarily includes purchased supply chain finance receivables and purchased auto loan securitizations in CIB.
- VIEs sponsored by third parties:
  - The Firm participates as derivative counterparty, liquidity provider, investor, underwriter, placement agent, remarketing agent, trustee, or custodian on an arm’s‑length basis.
  - Consolidation generally does not occur when the Firm lacks power over significant activities or does not hold a potentially significant variable interest; such positions are recorded like other third‑party transactions.
- Tax credit vehicles:
  - Investments as a limited partner in affordable housing, energy, and similar projects that are primarily VIEs; generally not consolidated due to third‑party control.
  - Returns are primarily via tax credits; risk mitigated by phasing capital until projects qualify for credits.
  - Maximum loss exposure: $32.4B at 6/30/23 ($12.6B unfunded) vs. $30.2B at 12/31/22 ($10.6B unfunded).

text:
VIEs sponsored by third parties
The Firm enters into transactions with VIEs structured by 
other parties. These include, for example, acting as a 
derivative counterparty, liquidity provider , investor , 
underwriter, placement agent, remarketing agent, trustee 
or custodian. These transactions are conducted at arm’s-
length, and individual credit decisions are based on the 
analysis of the specific VIE, taking into consideration the 
quality of the underlying assets. Where  the Firm does not 
have the power to direct the activities of the VIE that most 
significantly impact the VIE’s economic performance, or a 
variable interest that could potentially be significant,  the 
Firm generally does not consolidate the VIE, but it records 
and reports these positions on its Consolidated balance 
sheets in the same manner it would record and report 
positions in respect of any other third-party transaction.

text:
Tax credit vehicles 
The Firm  holds investments in unconsolidated tax credit 
vehicles, which are limited partnerships and similar entities 
that own and operate affordable housing , energy, and other  
projects. These entities are primarily considered VIEs. A 
third party is typically the general partner or managing member and has control over the significant activities of the 
tax credit vehicles, and accordingly  the Firm does not 
consolidate tax credit vehicles.  The Firm generally invests in 
these partnerships as a limited partner and earns a return 
primarily through the receipt of tax credits allocated to the 
projects. The maximum loss exposure, represented by 
equity investments and funding commitments, was  $32.4 
billion  and $30.2 billion  at J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 3, and 
D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  2 0 2 2, of which  $12.6 billion  and $10.6 
billion  was unfunded at  J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 3, and D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  
2022 , respectively.  The Firm assesses each project and to 
reduce the risk of loss, may withhold varying amounts of its 
capital investment until the project qualifies for tax credits. 
Refer to Note  25 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2022  Form 10-K for 
further information on affordable housing tax credits  and 
Note 24 of this Form 10-Q for more information on off-
balance sheet lending-related commitments.

The Firm may provide various services to customer TOB 
trusts, including  remarketing agent, liquidity or tender 
option provider. In certain customer TOB transactions,  the 
Firm, as liquidity provider, has entered into a 
reimbursement agreement with the Residual holder.

- Goodwill impairment testing approach: annual test in Q4 or interim if triggering events occur.

text:
Goodwill impairment testing
Goodwill is tested for impairment during the fourth quarter 
of each fiscal year, or more often if events or 
circumstances, such as adverse changes in the business 
climate, indicate that there may be an impairment.  Refer to 
Note  15 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2022  Form 10-K for a further 
discussion of  the Firm’s goodwill impairment testing.
Unanticipated declines in business performance, increases 
in credit losses, increases in capital requirements, as well as 
deterioration in economic or market conditions, adverse 
regulatory or legislative changes or increases in the 
estimated market cost of equity, could cause the estimated 
fair values of the  Firm’s reporting units to decline in the 
future, which could result in a material impairment charge 
to earnings in a future period related to some portion of the 
associated goodwill.  
As of  J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 3, the Firm reviewed current economic 
conditions, estimated market cost of equity, as well as 
actual business results and projections of business 
performance . Based on such reviews, the Firm has 
concluded that goodwill was not impaired as of J u n e  3 0 ,  
2023 , or D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  2 0 2 2, nor was goodwill written off 
due to impairment during the six months ended  J u n e  3 0 ,  
2023  or 2022 .

title: Mortgage servicing rights
heading: Mortgage servicing right s
start_phrase: MSRs represent the fair value of expected future cash flows for performing servicing activities for others.
summary:
- Defines mortgage servicing rights (MSRs) as the fair value of expected future cash flows from servicing loans for others, valued based on estimated fees and ancillary revenue less servicing costs; MSR fair value declines over time as servicing cash flows are realized (effective amortization).
- Explains recognition of MSRs when purchased or when loans are sold/securitized with servicing retained; references additional details in JPMorgan Chase’s 2022 Form 10-K (Notes 2 and 15).
- Summarizes MSR activity for the three and six months ended June 30, 2023 and 2022:
  - Beginning fair value (Q2 2023): $7.755B; ending fair value (6/30/23): $8.229B vs $7.439B (6/30/22).
  - Net additions in Q2 2023: $454MM (originations $78MM, purchases $468MM, dispositions $(92)MM); year-to-date net additions $487MM.
  - Reductions from collection/realization of expected cash flows: $(255)MM in Q2; $(495)MM YTD.
  - Valuation changes driven primarily by market interest rates and other factors: +$283MM in Q2; +$261MM YTD; minor impacts from other inputs/assumptions.
  - Unrealized gains/losses in income mirror valuation changes.
  - Footnotes detail purchase price adjustments for early prepayments, transfers of excess MSRs to agency trusts for SMBS, and definitions of rate-driven vs other prepayment effects.
- Provides servicing and balance metrics:
  - Contractual/ancillary fee income: $388MM in Q2 2023; $776MM YTD.
  - Third-party mortgage loans serviced: $605B at 6/30/23 (vs $576B prior year).
  - Servicer advances net of allowance: $595MM at 6/30/23 (vs $1.166B prior year); advances are generally reimbursable and senior in cash flow priority, with limited credit risk except if advances violate applicable rules/agreements.
- Details mortgage fees and related income (CCB):
  - Production revenue: $102MM in Q2 2023; $177MM YTD.
  - Net mortgage servicing revenue:
    - Operating revenue: loan servicing revenue $402MM less MSR cash flow realization $(255)MM = $147MM in Q2.
    - Risk management: MSR FV changes due to rates/other +$283MM; other model inputs $(8)MM; derivatives and other $(250)MM; net +$25MM in Q2.
    - Total net mortgage servicing revenue: $172MM in Q2; $320MM YTD.
  - Total CCB mortgage fees and related income: $274MM in Q2; $497MM YTD. Firmwide mortgage fees and related income: $278MM in Q2; $499MM YTD.
- Notes on valuation methodology and sensitivities:
  - Changes in assumptions are interrelated and non-linear; sensitivities shown are isolated, holding other inputs constant.
  - Key assumptions and sensitivities:
    - Weighted-average CPR: 6.27% at 6/30/23 (6.12% at 12/31/22); 10%/20% adverse CPR change reduces MSR FV by ~$186MM/~$361MM.
    - Weighted-average option-adjusted spread: 5.77% at both dates; 100bp/200bp adverse OAS change reduces MSR FV by ~$348MM/~$668MM (includes operational risk and regulatory capital).
text:
MSRs represent the fair value of expected future cash flows for performing servicing activities for others. The fair value 
considers estimated future servicing fees and ancillary revenue, offset by estimated costs to service the loans, and generally 
declines over time as net servicing cash flows are received, effectively amortizing the MSR asset against contractual servicing 
and ancillary fee income. MSRs are either purchased from third parties or recognized upon sale or securitization of mortgage 
loans if servicing is retained. Refer to Note s 2 and 15 of JPMorgan Chase ’s 2022  Form 10-K  for a further description of the 
MSR asset, interest rate risk management, and the valuation of MSRs.

heading: Note 18 – Long-term debt
start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase issues long-term debt denominated in various currencies, predominantly U.S. dollars, with both fixed and variable interest rates.
summary:
- Scope: Note 18 details JPMorgan Chase’s long-term debt profile and related practices; Note 19 summarizes outstanding non-cumulative preferred stock, dividend activity, and recent redemptions.

- Long-term debt overview (June 30, 2023 vs. December 31, 2022):
  - Total long-term debt rose to $364.1 billion from $295.9 billion.
  - Parent company subtotal: $215.5 billion (down from $225.8 billion), primarily senior fixed- and variable-rate debt plus subordinated fixed-rate debt.
  - Subsidiaries subtotal: $146.8 billion (up from $68.2 billion), reflecting:
    - Federal Home Loan Bank (FHLB) advances of $36.1 billion, including $25.0 billion tied to the First Republic acquisition.
    - A $48.9 billion fixed-rate Purchase Money Note (3.40%, maturing in 1–5 years) from the First Republic acquisition.
    - Additional senior fixed- and variable-rate borrowings; small amount of subordinated and junior subordinated debt.
  - Junior subordinated debt totaled $1.8 billion.

- Maturities and optional redemption:
  - Debt maturing in the 12-month periods ending June 30: 2024 $41.9B; 2025 $58.5B; 2026 $38.0B; 2027 $29.2B; 2028 $75.2B.
  - $191.7 billion of debt was callable at the Firm’s option as of June 30, 2023.

- Interest rates and hedging:
  - Weighted-average contractual rate (excludes structured notes at fair value): 3.45% at June 30, 2023 (3.26% at Dec. 31, 2022).
  - After derivatives (interest rate and cross-currency swaps) the modified weighted-average rate: 5.02% (4.89% at Dec. 31, 2022).
  - Reported interest rates in tables exclude effects of hedge accounting derivatives and structured notes at fair value.

- Valuation and structure:
  - Certain equity-linked/indexed instruments are carried at fair value with changes in principal transactions revenue; DVA-related unrealized gains/losses in OCI.
  - Long-term debt at fair value: $78.6B (vs. $72.3B).
  - Secured long-term debt: $87.7B secured by $221.2B of assets (vs. $13.8B secured by $208.3B).
  - Zero-coupon notes outstanding: $11.2B (aggregate principal at maturity $45.7B; may exceed principal at next call date).

- Beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs:
  - Long-term beneficial interests totaled $1.1B (down from $2.1B); excludes $18.5B of short-term commercial paper/other short-term interests.

- Guarantees and covenants:
  - JPMorgan Chase & Co. guarantees certain subsidiary long-term debt/structured notes: $34.5B (vs. $28.2B); pari passu with other unsecured, unsubordinated debt.
  - Unsecured debt has no rating-trigger or financial covenant provisions that accelerate payments, change maturities/structure, limit borrowings, or require collateral based on adverse credit events.

- Preferred stock (non-cumulative):
  - Outstanding: 2,740,375 depositary shares representing $27.4B carrying value, across fixed-rate and fixed-to-floating series.
  - Dividends: Quarterly declarations summarized; several series pay fixed coupons until earliest redemption date, then float.
  - Reference rate transition: After June 30, 2023, certain fixed-to-floating series transitioned from USD LIBOR to three-month Term SOFR plus a 0.26% spread adjustment and specified series spreads; one series references five-year CMT plus spread after reset.
  - Series-specific updates:
    - Series Q became floating as of May 1, 2023 (SOFR + 3.25%).
    - Series CC became floating as of Nov. 1, 2022 (SOFR + 2.58%).
  - Liquidation/redemption terms: $10,000 per share plus accrued but unpaid dividends; aggregate liquidation value $27.8B at June 30, 2023.
  - Recent redemptions: Series I ($2.9B) on Oct. 31, 2022; Series V ($2.5B) on Oct. 3, 2022; Series Z ($2.0B) on Feb. 1, 2022.

start_phrase: Refer to Note 23 of JPMorgan Chase ’s 2022 Form 10-K for a discussion of the computation of basic and diluted earnings per share (“EPS”).
summary:
- Scope: Note 20 – Earnings per share (EPS) for JPMorgan Chase, summarizing the calculation of basic and diluted EPS for the three and six months ended June 30, 2023 and 2022; methodology references Note 23 of the 2022 Form 10-K.
- Key components of EPS calculations:
  - Net income, less preferred stock dividends, to derive net income applicable to common equity.
  - Further reduction for dividends and undistributed earnings allocated to participating securities to arrive at net income applicable to common stockholders.
  - Weighted-average basic shares outstanding.
  - Diluted shares reflect the dilutive impact of unvested PSUs, nondividend-earning RSUs, and SARs.
- Results (in millions, except per share):
  - Q2 2023 vs Q2 2022:
    - Net income: $14,472 vs $8,649; preferred dividends: $373 vs $410.
    - Net income to common stockholders: $14,011 vs $8,195.
    - Basic shares: 2,943.8 vs 2,962.2; Basic EPS: $4.76 vs $2.77.
    - Dilutive impact: 4.5 vs 4.1; Diluted shares: 2,948.3 vs 2,966.3; Diluted EPS: $4.75 vs $2.76.
  - Six months 2023 vs 2022:
    - Net income: $27,094 vs $16,931; preferred dividends: $729 vs $807.
    - Net income to common stockholders: $26,204 vs $16,039.
    - Basic shares: 2,956.1 vs 2,969.6; Basic EPS: $8.86 vs $5.40.
    - Dilutive impact: 4.4 vs 4.1; Diluted shares: 2,960.5 vs 2,973.7; Diluted EPS: $8.85 vs $5.39.
- Highlights:
  - EPS (both basic and diluted) increased significantly year-over-year for both the quarter and year-to-date.
  - Weighted-average share counts declined modestly, and dilution from equity awards added approximately 4–5 million shares.

title: Accumulated other comprehensive income/(loss)
heading: Note 21 – Accumulated other comprehensive income/(loss)
start_phrase: AOCI includes the after-tax change in unrealized gains and losses on investment securities, foreign currency translation adjustments (including the impact of related derivatives), fair value changes of excluded components on fair value hedges, cash flow hedging activities, net gain/(loss) related to the Firm’s defined benefit pension and OPEB plans, and fair value option-elected liabilities arising from changes in the Firm’s own credit risk (DVA).
summary:
- Scope: Note 21 summarizes Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income/(Loss) (AOCI), detailing components, period changes, tax effects, and line-item reclassifications to the income statement.
- AOCI components: after-tax unrealized gains/losses on investment securities; foreign currency translation adjustments (including related hedges); fair value changes of excluded components in fair value hedges; cash flow hedging activities; net gains/losses of defined benefit pension and OPEB plans; and DVA on fair value option–elected liabilities (own credit risk).
- Periods covered: three and six months ended June 30, 2023 and 2022, with beginning balances, net changes, and ending balances by component.
- AOCI ending balance: $(14.29)B at June 30, 2023 vs $(14.37)B at June 30, 2022; slight improvement year over year.
- Q2 2023 OCI (after-tax): +$128M vs Q2 2022: $(4.80)B. Key Q2 2023 drivers: +$757M from investment securities; +$70M translation; +$11M fair value hedges; offset by $(497)M cash flow hedges, $(207)M DVA, $(6)M pension/OPEB.
- 1H 2023 OCI (after-tax): +$3.05B vs 1H 2022: $(14.29)B. Key 1H 2023 drivers: +$2.97B investment securities; +$267M translation; +$301M cash flow hedges; partially offset by $(415)M DVA, $(61)M pension/OPEB, $(10)M fair value hedges.
- Component patterns vs 2022: 2022 showed large negative unrealized losses on investment securities and cash flow hedges, partially offset by positive DVA; 2023 shows recovery in securities, smaller translation positives, and DVA losses.
- Detailed pre-tax, tax effect, and after-tax tables provided for each component for both Q2 and 1H of 2023 and 2022.
- Accounting changes/transfers: As of June 30, 2023 includes $(29)M after-tax net unamortized unrealized loss for HTM securities transferred to AFS under hedge accounting guidance adopted Jan 1, 2023. Also includes after-tax net unamortized unrealized losses from AFS-to-HTM transfers of $(1.1)B (2023) and $(1.4)B (2022).
- Reclassification disclosures:
  - Securities realized gains/losses reclassified to Investment securities gains/(losses).
  - Translation and related hedge reclassifications recorded in other income/expense; a small reclassification tied to the CIFM acquisition and net investment hedge loss noted in 1H 2023 (not material).
  - Fair value hedges reflect cross-currency swap basis spreads excluded from effectiveness testing; initial cost recognized in earnings via interest accrual.
  - Cash flow hedge reclassifications primarily affect noninterest revenue, net interest income, and compensation expense.
- Overall: AOCI improved modestly from June 2022 to June 2023, with 2023 OCI gains driven mainly by recovery in unrealized investment securities valuations and modest favorable translation effects, partly offset by DVA and hedge-related movements.

title: Restricted cash and other restricted assets
heading: Note 22 – Restricted cash and other restricted assets
start_phrase: Refer to Note 26 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2022 Form 10-K for a detailed discussion of the Firm’s restricted cash and other restricted assets.
summary:
- Note 22 – Restricted cash and other restricted assets:
  - Explains that certain Firm assets are restricted by U.S. and non-U.S. regulators, including limits tied to broker-dealer activities.
  - Breaks down restricted cash as of June 30, 2023 vs. December 31, 2022:
    - Segregated for securities and cleared derivatives customers: $17.0b vs. $18.7b.
    - Cash reserves at non-U.S. central banks/other purposes: $8.6b vs. $8.1b.
    - Total restricted cash: $25.6b vs. $26.8b.
    - Footnote: comprised of deposits with banks ($24.3b vs. $25.4b) and cash and due from banks ($1.3b vs. $1.4b).
  - Other restricted assets:
    - Cash and securities pledged with clearing organizations for customers: $36.9b vs. $42.4b.
    - Securities restricted related to customer activity (fair value): $23.4b vs. $31.7b.
  - References Note 26 of the 2022 Form 10-K for more detail.

- Note 23 – Regulatory capital:
  - Outlines capital requirements set by the Federal Reserve for the consolidated holding company and the OCC for the principal insured depository institution (IDI), JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.
  - States the Firm must meet minimum ratios for CET1, Tier 1, Total capital, Tier 1 leverage, and the Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR); noncompliance could trigger regulatory action. IDI subsidiaries are also subject to these requirements.
  - Presents risk-based ratio requirements and well-capitalized thresholds (as of June 30, 2023 and December 31, 2022):
    - Standardized (BHC): CET1 12.5%, Tier 1 14.0%, Total 16.0; (IDI): 7.0%, 8.5%, 10.5.
    - Advanced (BHC): CET1 11.0%, Tier 1 12.5%, Total 14.5; (IDI): 7.0%, 8.5%, 10.5.
    - Well-capitalized: (BHC) Tier 1 6.0%, Total 10.0; (IDI) CET1 6.5%, Tier 1 8.0%, Total 10.0.
    - Notes BHC requirements include minimums plus a 4.0% GSIB surcharge and a 4.0% stress capital buffer (Standardized) or 2.5% capital conservation buffer (Advanced); IDIs have a 2.5% conservation buffer and no GSIB surcharge. 2022 BHC Standardized requirements were slightly lower (12.0%, 13.5%, 15.5); Advanced 10.5%, 12.0%, 14.0.
  - Leverage-based requirements:
    - Tier 1 leverage: 4.0% (BHC and IDI); well-capitalized IDI threshold 5.0% (no BHC well-capitalized threshold).
    - SLR: 5.0% (BHC), 6.0% (IDI); reflects 3.0% minimum plus supplementary leverage buffers of 2.0% (BHC) and 3.0% (IDI); well-capitalized IDI threshold 6.0% (none for BHC).
  - CECL regulatory capital transition:
    - The $2.9b CECL capital benefit is being phased out 25% per year over three years starting Jan 1, 2022; $1.4b remained in CET1 as of June 30, 2023.
    - Effective Jan 1, 2023, 50% of other CECL transition adjustments were phased out, affecting Tier 2 capital, adjusted average assets, total leverage exposure, and RWA.
  - References Note 27 of the 2022 Form 10-K for further detail.

title: Regulatory capital - Introduction
heading: Note 23 – Regulatory capital
start_phrase: Refer to Note 27 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2022 Form 10-K for a detailed discussion on regulatory capital.
summary: Overview of JPMorgan Chase’s regulatory capital framework and required ratios as set by the Federal Reserve, OCC, and FDIC for the consolidated holding company and its IDI subsidiary, JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., with reference to Note 27 of the 2022 Form 10-K. It outlines minimum risk-based (CET1, Tier 1, Total capital) and leverage-based (Tier 1 leverage, SLR) requirements and notes that failure to meet them may prompt Federal Reserve action. Tables (as of June 30, 2023 and December 31, 2022) present: for the BHC, Basel III Standardized requirements of CET1 12.5%, Tier 1 14.0%, Total 16.0 and Advanced requirements of CET1 11.0%, Tier 1 12.5%, Total 14.5; for IDIs, CET1 7.0%, Tier 1 8.5%, Total 10.5; well-capitalized thresholds of CET1 NA/6.5% (BHC/IDI), Tier 1 6.0%/8.0%, Total 10.0%/10.0%. Leverage requirements: Tier 1 leverage 4.0% (BHC/IDI), SLR 5.0% (BHC) and 6.0% (IDI); well-capitalized thresholds apply to IDIs only (Tier 1 leverage 5.0%, SLR 6.0%). Footnotes specify buffers: Firm requirements include a 4.0% GSIB surcharge (Method 2), a 4.0% SCB for Standardized and a 2.5% capital conservation buffer for Advanced; countercyclical buffer is 0%; IDIs have a 2.5% capital conservation buffer and no GSIB surcharge; SLR includes a 3.0% minimum plus 2.0% (BHC) and 3.0% (IDI) supplementary buffers.
text:
Regulatory capital
Refer to Note 27 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2022  Form 10-K for 
a detailed discussion on regulatory capital.
The Federal Reserve establishes capital requirements, 
including well-capitalized requirements, for the 
consolidated financial holding company. The Office of the 
Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") establishes similar 
minimum capital requirements and standards for the Firm’s 
principal IDI subsidiary, JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. 
Under the risk-based capital and leverage-based guidelines 
of the Federal Reserve, JPMorgan Chase is required to 
maintain minimum ratios  for CET1 capital, Tier 1 capital, 
Total capital, Tier 1 leverage and the SLR . Failure to meet 
these minimum requirements  could cause the Federal 
Reserve to take action. IDI subsidiaries are also subject to 
these capital requirements  established by their respective 
primary regulators.

title: CECL regulatory capital transition
heading: CECL regulatory capital transition
start_phrase: Beginning January 1, 2022, the $ 2 . 9 b i l l i o n CECL capital benefit, provided by the Federal Reserve in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, is being phased out at 25% per year over a three-year period.
summary:
- Overview of U.S. regulatory capital requirements for JPMorgan Chase & Co. (BHC) and its insured depository institution (IDI) subsidiary, JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., under Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC rules, with reference to Note 27 of the 2022 Form 10-K for more detail.
- Presentation of risk-based capital ratio minimums and “well-capitalized” thresholds under Basel III Standardized and Advanced approaches:
  - BHC Standardized requirements: CET1 12.5%, Tier 1 14.0%, Total 16.0.
  - BHC Advanced requirements: CET1 11.0%, Tier 1 12.5%, Total 14.5.
  - IDI minimums: CET1 7.0%, Tier 1 8.5%, Total 10.5; IDI well-capitalized: CET1 6.5%, Tier 1 8.0%, Total 10.0.
  - Notes on buffers: 4.0% GSIB surcharge (BHC), 4.0% SCB for Standardized and 2.5% capital conservation buffer for Advanced; countercyclical buffer at 0%; IDIs are not subject to GSIB surcharge.
- Leverage-based capital requirements and well-capitalized thresholds:
  - Tier 1 leverage minimum 4.0% for BHC and IDI; IDI well-capitalized at 5.0%.
  - SLR minimums including buffers: 5.0% for BHC (3% base + 2% buffer) and 6.0% for IDI (3% base + 3% buffer); well-capitalized IDI SLR at 6.0%; no well-capitalized thresholds for BHC leverage ratios.
- CECL regulatory capital transition:
  - COVID-related $2.9 billion CET1 benefit being phased out at 25% per year beginning 2022; $1.4 billion remained in CET1 at June 30, 2023.

title: Off–balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees, and other commitments - Introduction
heading: Note 24 – Off–balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees, and other commitments
start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase provides lending-related financial instruments (e.g., commitments and guarantees) to address the financing needs of its customers and clients.
summary: This section describes JPMorgan Chase’s off–balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees, and other commitments, noting that contractual amounts reflect maximum possible credit risk but are typically not fully utilized; an allowance for credit losses on lending-related commitments is maintained (see Notes 13 and 28). It presents a maturity-dated table of contractual amounts and carrying values as of June 30, 2023 and December 31, 2022 covering consumer (credit card $881.5bn; residential real estate $34.0bn; auto/other $16.8bn; total consumer $932.3bn), wholesale (other unfunded commitments $509.3bn; standby letters of credit/financial guarantees $28.4bn; other letters of credit $3.4bn; total wholesale $541.1bn), and totals (total lending-related $1.473tn; carrying value $5.054bn vs $1.327tn and $2.817bn in 2022). Other guarantees/commitments include securities lending indemnification agreements $296.5bn (collateral held $312.6bn), derivatives qualifying as guarantees $56.9bn, unsettled resale/borrowed $109.1bn, unsettled repo/loaned $93.4bn, exchange and clearing house guarantees $140.1bn, loans sold with recourse $768m (carrying $27m), mortgage repurchase liability (carrying $76m), and other guarantees $11.2bn. Key practices and qualifiers include: most amounts are U.S.-based; amounts for certain items are shown net of risk participations; carrying value reflects allowances/guarantee liabilities or fair value; the Firm can reduce/cancel credit card and certain business banking lines (typically closes cards at 60+ days past due) and may reduce/close HELOCs on property value or credit deterioration; and June 30, 2023 figures include fair value adjustments from the First Republic acquisition ($576m residential RE, $236m auto/other, $1.6bn other unfunded commitments) and bridge financing markdowns.
text:
Off–balance sheet lending-related 
financial instruments, guarantees, and other 
commitments
JPMorgan Chase  provides lending-related financial 
instruments (e.g., commitments and guarantees) to address 
the financing needs of its customers and clients. The 
contractual amount of these financial instruments 
represents the maximum possible credit risk to  the Firm 
should the customer or client draw upon the commitment 
or the Firm  be required to fulfill its obligation under the 
guarantee, and should the customer or client subsequently 
fail to perform according to the terms of the contract. Most 
of these commitments and guarantees have historically 
been refinanced, extended, cancelled, or expired without 
being drawn or a default occurring. As a result, the total 
contractual amount of these instruments is not, in  the 
Firm’s view, representative of its expected future credit 
exposure or funding requirements.  Refer to Note  28 of 
JPMorgan Chase ’s 2022  Form 10-K  for a further discussion 
of lending-related commitments and guarantees, and the  
Firm’s related accounting policies.  
To provide for expected  credit losses in wholesale and 
certain consumer lending-related commitments, an 
allowance for credit losses on lending-related commitments 
is maintained. Refer to Note  13 for further information 
regarding the allowance for credit losses on lending-related 
commitments .The following table summarizes the contractual amounts 
and carrying values of off-balance sheet lending-related 
financial instruments, guarantees and other commitments 
at J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 3, and D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  2 0 2 2. The amounts in 
the table below for credit card, home equity and certain 
scored business banking lending-related commitments 
represent the total available credit for these products.  The 
Firm has not experienced, and does not anticipate, that all 
available lines of credit for these products will be utilized at 
the same time.  The Firm can reduce or cancel credit card 
and certain scored business banking lines of credit by 
providing the borrower notice or, in some cases as 
permitted by law, without notice. In addition,  the Firm 
typically closes credit card lines when the borrower is  60 
days  or more past due.  The Firm may reduce or close 
HELOCs when there are significant decreases in the value of 
the underlying property, or when there has been a 
demonstrable decline in the creditworthiness of the 
borrower.

title: Other unfunded commitments to extend credit
heading: Other unfunded commitments to extend credit
start_phrase: Other unfunded commitments to extend credit generally consist of commitments for working capital and general corporate purposes, extensions of credit to support commercial paper facilities and bond financings in the event that those obligations cannot be remarketed to new investors, as well as committed liquidity facilities to clearing organizations.
summary:
- Scope: Disclosures on off–balance sheet exposures, including other unfunded commitments to extend credit, standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees, derivatives that qualify as guarantees, and merchant charge-back contingencies.

- Other unfunded commitments: Primarily working capital and general corporate purpose facilities, backstop liquidity for commercial paper and bond financings when remarketing fails, and committed liquidity facilities to clearing organizations. Includes multipurpose facilities that may be drawn as standby letters of credit.

- Standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees: Conditional lending commitments guaranteeing client performance to third parties for uses such as CP backstops, bond and acquisition financings, trade financings, etc.

- Credit quality reference: Investment-grade and noninvestment-grade classifications are based on the Firm’s internal risk ratings (referenced Note 12).

- Quantitative summary (June 30, 2023 vs. December 31, 2022):
  - Total contractual amounts:
    - Standby LCs and other financial guarantees: $28,406mm (vs. $27,439mm)
    - Other letters of credit: $3,361mm (vs. $4,134mm)
    - By rating (6/30/23): Investment-grade $19,574mm + $2,385mm; Noninvestment-grade $8,832mm + $976mm
  - Loss protection and carrying values:
    - Allowance for lending-related commitments: $146mm (vs. $82mm); Other LCs $23mm (vs. $6mm)
    - Guarantee liability: $371mm (vs. $326mm)
    - Total carrying value: $517mm and $23mm (vs. $408mm and $6mm)
  - Commitments with collateral: $16,414mm and $549mm (vs. $15,296mm and $795mm)

- Derivatives qualifying as guarantees (referenced Note 28):
  - Notional amounts (6/30/23 vs. 12/31/22):
    - Derivative guarantees: $56,900mm (vs. $59,180mm)
    - Stable value contracts (contractually limited exposure): $31,715mm (vs. $31,820mm)
    - Maximum exposure on stable value contracts: $1,442mm (vs. $2,063mm)
  - Fair value derivative payables: $181mm (vs. $649mm)
  - Note: The Firm is both a purchaser and seller of credit protection in the credit derivatives market (referenced Note 5).

- Merchant charge-backs: As a merchant acquirer, the Firm retains contingent liability for disputed card transactions. If unrecoverable from the merchant, the Firm bears the loss. Risk is mitigated via withheld settlements, cash reserves, collateral, and a recognized valuation allowance for payment/performance risk.

title: Merchant charge-backs
heading: Merchant charge-backs
start_phrase: Under the rules of payment networks, in its role as a merchant acquirer, the Firm's Merchant Services business in CIB Payments, retains a contingent liability for disputed processed credit and debit card transactions that result in a charge-back to the merchant.

- Merchant charge-backs (CIB Payments merchant acquiring):
  - Retains contingent liability for disputed card transactions resulting in charge-backs.

  - A valuation allowance is recognized for payment/performance risk related to charge-backs.
text:
Merchant charge-backs  
Under the rules of payment networks,  in its role as a 
merchant acquirer, the Firm's Merchant Services business 
in CIB Payments, retains a contingent liability for disputed 
processed credit and debit card transactions that result in a 
charge-back to the merchant. If a dispute is resolved in the 
cardholder’s favor, the Firm will (through the cardholder’s 
issuing bank) credit or refund the amount to the cardholder 
and will charge back the transaction to the merchant. If the 
Firm is unable to collect the amount from the merchant, the 
Firm will bear the loss for the amount credited or refunded 
to the cardholder. The Firm mitigates this risk by 
withholding future settlements, retaining cash reserve 
accounts or obtaining other collateral.  In addition, the Firm 
recognizes a valuation allowance that covers the payment 
or performance risk  related to charge-back s.

text:
Sponsored member repo program  
The Firm acts as a sponsoring member to clear eligible 
overnight and term resale and repurchase agreements 
through the Government Securities Division of the Fixed 
Income Clearing Corporation (“FICC”) on behalf of clients 
that become sponsored members under the FICC’s rules. 
The Firm also guarantees to the FICC the prompt and full 
payment and performance of its sponsored member clients’ 
respective obligations under the FICC’s rules. The  Firm 
minimizes its liability under these guarantees by obtaining a 
security interest in the cash or high-quality securities 
collateral that the clients place with the clearing house 
therefore the  Firm expects the risk of loss to be remote. The  
Firm’s maximum possible exposure, without taking into 
consideration the associated collateral, is included in the 
Exchange & clearing house guarantees and commitments 
line on  page 185 . Refer to Note  11 of JPMorgan Chase’s 
2022  Form 10-K  for additional information on credit risk 
mitigation practices on resale agreements and the types of 
collateral pledged under repurchase agreements.
