title: Contingencies
heading: Contingencies
start_phrase: As of June 30, 2023, the Firm and its subsidiaries and affiliates are defendants or respondents in numerous legal proceedings, including private, civil litigations, government investigations or regulatory enforcement matters.
summary:
- Overview: Note 26 – Litigation outlines the Firm’s legal contingencies as of June 30, 2023, covering numerous private civil litigations, government investigations, and regulatory enforcement matters across all lines of business and geographies, ranging from single-plaintiff cases to large class actions and involving claims such as common law tort, contract, antitrust, securities, and consumer protection.

- Loss estimates: The Firm estimates the aggregate range of reasonably possible losses in excess of established reserves at $0 to approximately $1.3 billion as of June 30, 2023. Not all matters are presently estimable. The estimate involves significant judgment due to the number and stages of proceedings, multiple defendants, unresolved issues (e.g., class certification, claim scope), and uncertain outcomes. Actual losses may differ materially and estimates may change over time.

- Material proceedings:
  - 1MDB Litigation: J.P. Morgan (Suisse) SA was sued in Malaysia in May 2021 for alleged “dishonest assistance” related to 2009–2010 transfers of $300 million and $500 million into a 1MDB PetroSaudi Limited account at J.P. Morgan Suisse. The Firm challenged service and jurisdiction in September 2022. In April 2023, 1MDB discontinued its claim against J.P. Morgan (Suisse) SA while seeking court permission to potentially refile; the court took the request under consideration.
  - Amrapali (India): The Enforcement Directorate (ED) is investigating J.P. Morgan India Private Limited regarding 2010 and 2012 investments by two offshore funds into Amrapali residential projects. Civil claims by creditors and home buyers (overseen by India’s Supreme Court) are ongoing. The ED fined J.P. Morgan India approximately $31.5 million in August 2021; the Firm is appealing. In July 2019, the Supreme Court made preliminary findings indicating violations by Amrapali and others (including unspecified JPMorgan entities and the offshore funds) and ordered further ED inquiries under PMLA and FEMA. In May 2020, the ED attached about $25 million from J.P. Morgan India Private Limited. The Firm is responding to and cooperating with the PMLA investigation.
  - Foreign Exchange matters: The Firm previously settled with authorities over FX sales and trading activities and related controls; in May 2015 it pleaded guilty to a single federal antitrust violation. The Department of Labor granted exemptions allowing continued reliance on the ERISA QPAM exemption.
text:
Contingencies 
As of June 30, 2023, the Firm and its subsidiaries and 
affiliates are defendants or respondents in numerous legal 
proceedings, including private, civil litigations, government 
investigations or regulatory enforcement matters. The 
litigations range from individual actions involving a single 
plaintiff to class action lawsuits with potentially millions of 
class members. Investigations and regulatory enforcement 
matters involve both formal and informal proceedings, by 
both governmental agencies and self-regulatory 
organizations. These legal proceedings are at varying stages 
of adjudication, arbitration or investigation, and involve 
each of the Firm’s lines of business and several geographies 
and a wide variety of claims (including common law tort 
and contract claims and statutory antitrust, securities and 
consumer protection claims), some of which present novel 
legal theories.
The Firm believes the estimate of the aggregate range of 
reasonably possible losses, in excess of reserves 
established, for its legal proceedings is from $0 to 
approximately  $ 1 . 3  b i l l i o n at June 30, 2023. This 
estimated aggregate range of reasonably possible losses 
was based upon information available as of that date for 
those proceedings in which the Firm believes that an 
estimate of reasonably possible loss can be made. For 
certain matters, the Firm does not believe that such an 
estimate can be made, as of that date. The Firm’s estimate 
of the aggregate range of reasonably possible losses 
involves significant judgment, given:
•the number, variety and varying stages of the 
proceedings, including the fact that many are in 
preliminary stages, 
•the existence in many such proceedings of multiple 
defendants, including the Firm, whose share of liability 
(if any) has yet to be determined, 
•the numerous yet-unresolved issues in many of the 
proceedings, including issues regarding class 
certification and the scope of many of the claims, and 
•the uncertainty of the various potential outcomes of 
such proceedings, including where the Firm has made 
assumptions concerning future rulings by the court or 
other adjudicator, or about the behavior or incentives of 
adverse parties or regulatory authorities, and those 
assumptions prove to be incorrect.
In addition, the outcome of a particular proceeding may be 
a result which the Firm did not take into account in its 
estimate because the Firm had deemed the likelihood of 
that outcome to be remote. Accordingly, the Firm’s 
estimate of the aggregate range of reasonably possible 
losses will change from time to time, and actual losses may 
vary significantly.Set forth below are descriptions of the Firm’s material legal 
proceedings.

jurisdiction to hear the claim. In April 2023, 1MDB 
discontinued its claim against J.P. Morgan (Suisse) SA, but 
requested permission of the Court to refile in the future, 
which the Court took under consideration.

summary:
- Scope and nature of litigation: As of June 30, 2023, the Firm faces numerous legal proceedings across all lines of business and geographies, including private civil actions (individual and class), government investigations, and regulatory enforcement matters, involving claims such as tort, contract, antitrust, securities, and consumer protection, some with novel legal theories.

- Loss contingency estimate: Aggregate range of reasonably possible losses in excess of reserves is $0 to approximately $1.3 billion at June 30, 2023. Not all matters are estimable. The estimate is highly judgmental due to early case stages, multiple defendants, unresolved issues (e.g., class certification, claim scope), and uncertain outcomes; actual losses may differ significantly and estimates will change over time.

- 1MDB litigation (Malaysia): J.P. Morgan (Suisse) SA accused of “dishonest assistance” related to $300 million (2009) and $500 million (2010) payments involving a 1MDB joint venture account. The Firm challenged service and jurisdiction; in April 2023, 1MDB discontinued its claim but sought leave to refile.

- Amrapali (India): ED investigating J.P. Morgan India regarding 2010/2012 investments by offshore funds in Amrapali Group housing projects. ED imposed an approximately $31.5 million fine in August 2021 (under appeal). The Supreme Court of India made preliminary findings in 2019 regarding currency control and money laundering violations and directed further inquiries under PMLA and FEMA. In May 2020, ED attached approximately $25 million from J.P. Morgan India. The Firm is cooperating.

- Foreign exchange (FX) investigations and litigation:
  - Governmental: Prior settlements; in May 2015, the Firm pleaded guilty to a single federal antitrust violation. DOL granted ERISA QPAM exemptions during the ten-year disqualification period. Remaining inquiry: South Africa Competition Commission matter pending before the Competition Tribunal.
  - Civil: U.S. consolidated class action settlement approved (Aug 2018; final approval previously granted). Opt-out claims largely resolved (Dec 2022). Another U.S. putative class was denied certification and summary judgment entered for defendants (Mar 2023); appeal filed. Additional actions outside the U.S. in the U.K., Israel, Netherlands, Brazil, and Australia; one U.K. action resolved (Dec 2022); U.K. Court of Appeal (Jul 2023) overturned denial of opt-out class certification; settlement in principle in Israel pending court approval.

- Interchange litigation:
  - Monetary class: Amended settlement (Sep 2018) added $900 million to the ~$5.3 billion escrow from the original settlement; District Court approval (Dec 2019) affirmed by the Second Circuit (Mar 2023); rehearing petitions filed. Based on opt-outs, $700 million was returned to defendants.
  - Injunctive class: Certification granted in part and denied in part (Sep 2021); case continues.
  - Opt-out merchant actions: Many individual cases settled; settlements cover approximately 65% of combined Mastercard- and Visa-branded sales volume.

- Jeffrey Epstein litigation (SDNY): JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. sued by an alleged victim class (Nov 2022) and by the U.S. Virgin Islands (Dec 2022) alleging it knowingly facilitated Epstein’s activities. Court granted in part/denied in part motions to dismiss (Mar 2023). The Bank impleaded former employee James Edward Staley; his motion to dismiss was denied (May 2023). Class certification granted and preliminary approval of a $290 million settlement for Epstein survivors (Jun 2023). USVI and Staley actions continue.

- LIBOR and other benchmarks: The Firm has responded to global inquiries related to LIBOR and EURIBOR. Swiss Competition Commission’s EURIBOR investigation continues. The European Commission’s 2016 decision finding antitrust infringement related to EURIBOR (against the Firm and others) is under appeal before the European General Court.
text:
Foreign Exchange Investigations and Litigation.  The Firm 
previously reported settlements with certain government 
authorities relating to its foreign exchange (“FX”) sales and 
trading activities and controls related to those activities. 
Among those resolutions, in May 2015, the Firm pleaded 
guilty to a single violation of federal antitrust law. The 
Department of Labor ("DOL") granted the Firm exemptions 
that permit the Firm and its affiliates to continue to rely on 
the Qualified Professional Asset Manager exemption under 
the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (“ERISA”) 
188through the ten-year  disqualification period following the 
antitrust plea. The only remaining FX-related governmental 
inquiry is a South Africa Competition Commission matter 
which is currently pending before the South Africa 
Competition Tribunal.
With respect to civil litigation matters, in August 2018, the 
United States District Court for the Southern District of New 
York granted final approval to the Firm’s settlement of a 
consolidated class action brought by U.S.-based plaintiffs, 
which principally alleged violations of federal antitrust laws 
based on an alleged conspiracy to manipulate foreign 
exchange rates and also sought damages on behalf of 
persons who transacted in FX futures and options on 
futures. Although certain members of the settlement class 
filed requests to the Court to be excluded from the class, an 
agreement to resolve their claims was reached in December 
2022. The District Court denied certification of a putative 
class action against the Firm and other foreign exchange 
dealers on behalf of certain parties who purchased foreign 
currencies at allegedly inflated rates and granted summary 
judgment against the named plaintiffs in March 2023.  
Those plaintiffs have filed a notice of appeal. In addition, 
some FX-related individual and putative class actions based 
on similar alleged underlying conduct have been filed 
outside the U.S., including in the U.K., Israel, the 
Netherlands, Brazil and Australia. An agreement to resolve 
one of the UK actions was reached in December 2022. In 
July 2023, the U.K. Court of Appeal overturned the 
Competition Appeal Tribunal's earlier denial of a request for 
class certification on an opt-out basis. In Israel, a settlement 
in principle has been reached in the putative class action, 
which remains subject to court approval.

title: Interchange Litigation
heading: Interchange Litigation
start_phrase: Groups of merchants and retail associations filed a series of class action complaints alleging that Visa and Mastercard, as well as certain banks, conspired to set the price of credit and debit card interchange fees and enacted related rules in violation of antitrust laws.
summary:
- Foreign exchange (FX) matters: Only remaining governmental inquiry is before the South Africa Competition Commission. In the U.S., a consolidated class action settlement was approved in 2018; opt-out claims were resolved in December 2022. Certification of a separate putative class was denied and summary judgment entered for defendants in March 2023; plaintiffs appealed. Similar actions have been filed outside the U.S. (U.K., Israel, Netherlands, Brazil, Australia). A U.K. action was settled in December 2022; in July 2023, the U.K. Court of Appeal reinstated an opt-out class certification request. In Israel, a settlement in principle awaits court approval.
- Interchange litigation: Merchants alleged Visa/Mastercard and certain banks fixed credit/debit interchange fees. After an initial settlement was reversed, the case was split into monetary and injunctive classes. An amended monetary settlement added $900 million to $5.3 billion and was approved in 2019; the Second Circuit affirmed in March 2023, with rehearing petitions pending. Due to opt-outs, $700 million was returned to defendants. The injunctive class was certified in part in 2021. Some opt-out merchants filed individual suits; settlements cover about 65% of combined Visa/Mastercard sales volume.
- Jeffrey Epstein litigation: JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. was sued in SDNY by an alleged victim class and by the U.S. Virgin Islands, alleging the bank facilitated Epstein’s misconduct. In March 2023, parts of both cases were allowed to proceed; JPMorgan impleaded former employee James Edward Staley, and his motion to dismiss was denied in May 2023. In June 2023, the court certified the victim class and preliminarily approved a $290 million settlement for survivors. The USVI action and claims against Staley continue.
- LIBOR/EURIBOR investigations: Ongoing responses to global inquiries concerning LIBOR and EURIBOR. The Swiss Competition Commission’s EURIBOR investigation continues. The European Commission issued a 2016 decision finding EURIBOR-related antitrust infringements against the firm and others; the firm’s appeal to the European General Court remains pending.
text:
Interchange Litigation. Groups of merchants and retail 
associations filed a series of class action complaints alleging 
that Visa and Mastercard, as well as certain banks, 
conspired to set the price of credit and debit card 
interchange fees and enacted related rules in violation of 
antitrust laws. In 2012, the parties initially settled the cases 
for a cash payment, but that settlement was reversed on 
appeal and remanded to the United States District Court for 
the Eastern District of New York.
The original class action was divided into two separate 
actions, one seeking primarily monetary relief and the other 
seeking primarily injunctive relief. In September 2018, the 
parties to the monetary class action finalized an agreement 
which amends and supersedes the prior settlement 
agreement. Pursuant to this settlement, the defendants 
collectively contributed an additional $900 million  to the 
approximately $5.3 billion  previously held in escrow from 
the original settlement. In December 2019, the amended 
settlement agreement was approved by the District Court. 
In March 2023, the United States Court of Appeals for the 
Second Circuit affirmed the District Court’s approval of the 
settlement, and two merchants have filed petitions for 
rehearing of the Appellate Court’s approval. Based on the 
percentage of merchants that opted out of the amended 
class settlement, $700 million  has been returned to the defendants from the settlement escrow in accordance with 
the settlement agreement. The injunctive class action 
continues separately, and in September 2021, the District 
Court granted plaintiffs’ motion for class certification in 
part, and denied the motion in part.
Of the merchants who opted out of the amended damages 
class settlement, certain merchants filed individual actions 
raising similar allegations against Visa and Mastercard, as 
well as against the Firm and other banks. While some of 
those actions remain pending, the defendants have reached 
settlements with the merchants who opted out representing 
approximately 65%  of the combined Mastercard-branded 
and Visa-branded payment card sales volume.

title: Jeffrey Epstein Litigation
heading: Jeffrey Epstein Litigation
start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. was named as a defendant in two lawsuits filed in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York alleging that JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. knowingly facilitated Jeffrey Epstein’s sex trafficking and other unlawful conduct by providing banking services to Epstein until 2013.
summary:
- Foreign exchange (FX) matters: Reference to a ten-year disqualification period following an antitrust plea; the only remaining FX-related governmental inquiry is a South Africa Competition Commission case pending before the South Africa Competition Tribunal. In civil litigation, a U.S. consolidated class action settlement received final approval in August 2018; exclusions were resolved in December 2022. In March 2023, a U.S. District Court denied class certification and granted summary judgment against named plaintiffs, who have appealed. Similar actions outside the U.S. are pending in the U.K., Israel, the Netherlands, Brazil, and Australia; one U.K. action was resolved in December 2022, the U.K. Court of Appeal reinstated opt-out certification in July 2023, and a settlement in principle in Israel awaits court approval.
- Interchange litigation: Merchants alleged Visa, Mastercard, and certain banks fixed credit/debit interchange fees and adopted anticompetitive rules. After an initial 2012 settlement was reversed, the case was split into monetary and injunctive tracks. An amended monetary settlement in 2018 added $900 million to $5.3 billion in escrow; it was approved in December 2019 and affirmed by the Second Circuit in March 2023, with rehearing petitions filed. Due to opt-outs, $700 million was returned to defendants. The injunctive case remains, with class certification granted in part in September 2021. Individual opt-out suits continue, though settlements have been reached with merchants representing about 65% of combined Visa/Mastercard sales volume.
- Jeffrey Epstein litigation: Two SDNY suits allege JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. knowingly facilitated Epstein’s trafficking by providing banking services (a November 2022 putative class action by an alleged victim and a December 2022 action by the U.S. Virgin Islands). In March 2023, the court allowed some claims to proceed. JPMorgan impleaded former employee James Edward Staley for indemnification and related claims; his motion to dismiss was denied in May 2023. In June 2023, the court certified the class and preliminarily approved a $290 million settlement for survivors. The USVI and Staley actions continue.

text:
Jeffrey Epstein Litigation.  JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. was 
named as a defendant in two lawsuits filed in the United 
States District Court for the Southern District of New York 
alleging that JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. knowingly 
facilitated Jeffrey Epstein’s sex trafficking and other 
unlawful conduct by providing banking services to Epstein 
until 2013. One case, which was filed in November 2022, 
was a putative class action filed by an alleged sex-
trafficking victim of Epstein, and the other case, which was 
filed in December 2022, was brought on behalf of the 
government of the United States Virgin Islands and also 
alleges certain Virgin Islands statutory claims. In March 
2023, the Court granted in part and denied in part 
JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.’s motions to dismiss these 
complaints, allowing some claims to proceed in both 
lawsuits. Also in March 2023, JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. 
filed third-party complaints impleading the Firm’s former 
employee, James Edward Staley, into the two lawsuits, 
asserting claims for indemnification, contribution, breach of 
fiduciary duty and violation of the faithless servant 
doctrine. In May 2023, the Court denied Staley’s motion to 
dismiss the impleader complaints. In June 2023, the Court 
granted the putative class’  motion for class certification and 
granted a preliminary approval of a settlement between the 
class and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., pursuant to which 
JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. will pay $ 2 9 0  m i l l i o n to a fund 
for Epstein survivors. The actions involving the government 
of the United States Virgin Islands and Staley are 
proceeding.

title: LIBOR and Other Benchmark Rate Investigations and Litigation
heading: LIBOR and Other Benchmark Rate Investigations and Litigation

text:
LIBOR and Other Benchmark Rate Investigations and 
Litigation.  JPMorgan Chase has responded to inquiries from 
various governmental agencies and entities around the 
world relating primarily to the British Bankers Association’s 
(“BBA”) London Interbank Offered Rate (“LIBOR”) for 
various currencies and the European Banking Federation’s 
Euro Interbank Offered Rate (“EURIBOR”). The Swiss 
Competition Commission’s investigation relating to 
EURIBOR, to which the Firm and one other bank remain 
subject, continues. In December 2016, the European 
Commission issued a decision against the Firm and other 
banks finding an infringement of European antitrust rules 
relating to EURIBOR. The Firm has filed an appeal of that 
decision with the European General Court, and that appeal 
is pending.
189In addition, the Firm has been named as a defendant along 
with other banks in various individual and putative class 
actions related to benchmark rates, including U.S. dollar 
LIBOR. In actions related to U.S. dollar LIBOR during the 
period that it was administered by the BBA, the Firm has 
obtained dismissal of certain actions and resolved certain 
other actions, and others are in various stages of litigation. 
The United States District Court for the Southern District of 
New York has granted class certification of antitrust claims 
related to bonds and interest rate swaps sold directly by the 
defendants, including the Firm. A consolidated putative 
class action related to the period that U.S. dollar LIBOR was 
administered by ICE Benchmark Administration has been 
dismissed. In addition, a group of individual plaintiffs filed a 
lawsuit asserting antitrust claims, alleging that the Firm and 
other defendants were engaged in an unlawful agreement 
to set U.S. dollar LIBOR and conspired to monopolize the 
market for LIBOR-based consumer loans and credit cards. In 
September 2022, the Court dismissed plaintiffs' complaint 
in its entirety, and plaintiffs filed an amended complaint 
asserting similar antitrust claims, which defendants have 
moved to dismiss. The Firm’s settlements of putative class 
actions related to the Singapore Interbank Offered Rate and 
the Singapore Swap Offer Rate, and the Australian Bank Bill 
Swap Reference Rate received final court approval in 
November 2022, while the settlement related to Swiss 
franc LIBOR remains subject to court approval.

title: Securities Lending Antitrust Litigation
heading: Securities Lending Antitrust Litigation
start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., J.P. Morgan Securities LLC, J.P. Morgan Prime, Inc., and J.P. Morgan Strategic Securities Lending Corp. are named as defendants in a putative class action filed in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York.
summary:
- Overview of JPMorgan Chase’s significant ongoing and resolved legal matters, primarily antitrust, benchmark rate litigation, securities lending, and shareholder actions.
- Benchmark rate cases:
  - Involvement as a defendant in individual and putative class actions tied to benchmark rates, including U.S. dollar LIBOR.
  - For the BBA-administered LIBOR period: some actions dismissed, others resolved, and remaining cases in various litigation stages; SDNY granted class certification of antitrust claims related to bonds and interest rate swaps sold directly by defendants, including the Firm.
  - For the ICE-administered LIBOR period: a consolidated putative class action was dismissed.
  - A separate group of individual plaintiffs alleged an antitrust conspiracy to set U.S. dollar LIBOR and monopolize markets for LIBOR-based consumer loans and credit cards; the complaint was dismissed in September 2022; plaintiffs filed an amended complaint and defendants moved to dismiss.
  - Settlements of putative class actions related to SIBOR/SOR and BBSW received final court approval in November 2022; a Swiss franc LIBOR settlement remains subject to court approval.
- Securities Lending Antitrust Litigation (SDNY):
  - JPMorgan entities named in a putative class action alleging a conspiracy to block anonymous exchange trading in securities lending.
  - Motion to dismiss denied; plaintiffs moved for class certification (opposed by defendants).
  - Parties reached an agreement in principle to settle, subject to documentation and court approval.
- Shareholder litigation:
  - Multiple putative class and derivative actions against the Firm, its Board, and certain current/former officers.
  - Matters tied to historical trading practices in precious metals and U.S. Treasuries (subject of 2020 DOJ, CFTC, SEC resolutions) and fiduciary activities (subject of a 2020 OCC resolution).
    - NY state derivative suit (filed May 2022) dismissed in December 2022; plaintiff appealed in January 2023.
    - EDNY derivative suit (filed December 2022) asserting breach of fiduciary duty and contribution; defendants moved to dismiss.
    - Consolidated putative securities class action (EDNY) alleging SEC filings were materially false or misleading for not disclosing certain trading practices; defendants moved to dismiss the amended complaint.
  - Records preservation oversight derivative suit (EDNY, filed March 2022) based on alleged Board oversight failures tied to SEC/CFTC resolutions; motion to dismiss pending.
  - Two SDNY derivative suits (May/June 2023) alleging failures by the Board and James Dimon regarding banking services to Jeffrey Epstein; actions consolidated; defendants moved to dismiss the amended complaint.
- General disclosures:
  - The Firm and its subsidiaries are involved in numerous additional legal proceedings; it asserts meritorious defenses and intends to defend vigorously; new proceedings may arise.
  - The Firm has established reserves for several hundred outstanding legal proceedings and accrues litigation liabilities in accordance with U.S. GAAP when a loss is probable.
text:
Securities Lending Antitrust Litigation . JPMorgan Chase 
Bank, N.A., J.P. Morgan Securities LLC, J.P. Morgan Prime, 
Inc., and J.P. Morgan Strategic Securities Lending Corp. are 
named as defendants in a putative class action filed in the 
United States District Court for the Southern District of New 
York. The complaint asserts violations of federal antitrust 
law and New York State common law in connection with an 
alleged conspiracy to prevent the emergence of anonymous 
exchange trading for securities lending transactions. 
Defendants’ motion to dismiss the complaint was denied. 
Plaintiffs have moved to certify a class in this action, which 
defendants have opposed. The parties have reached an 
agreement in principle to settle this action, subject to final 
documentation and court approval.

title: Shareholder Litigation
heading: Shareholder Litigation
start_phrase: Several shareholder putative class actions, as well as shareholder derivative actions purporting to act on behalf of the Firm, have been filed against the Firm, its Board of Directors and certain of its current and former officers.
summary:
- Benchmark rate litigation: JPMorgan Chase is a defendant in multiple individual and putative class actions tied to benchmark rates, including USD LIBOR. For the BBA-administered USD LIBOR period, some actions have been dismissed or resolved, others continue; the SDNY certified antitrust classes for bonds and interest rate swaps sold directly by defendants. A consolidated putative class action for the ICE-administered USD LIBOR period was dismissed. An individual-plaintiff antitrust suit alleging collusion to set USD LIBOR and monopolize LIBOR-based consumer loans/credit cards was dismissed in September 2022; plaintiffs filed an amended complaint that defendants moved to dismiss. Settlements for class actions related to SIBOR/SOR and BBSW received final approval in November 2022; a settlement related to CHF LIBOR remains subject to court approval.
- Securities Lending Antitrust Litigation: Several JPMorgan entities are defendants in a putative SDNY class action alleging an antitrust conspiracy to block anonymous exchange trading in securities lending. Motion to dismiss was denied; plaintiffs moved for class certification, which defendants opposed. The parties reached an agreement in principle to settle, subject to documentation and court approval.
- Shareholder litigation: Multiple shareholder putative class and derivative actions have been filed against the Firm, its Board, and current/former officers.
  - Matters related to historical precious metals and U.S. Treasuries trading practices and fiduciary activities resolved with DOJ/CFTC/SEC (Sept 2020) and OCC (Nov 2020): a NY state derivative suit was dismissed in Dec 2022; appeal filed Jan 2023. An EDNY derivative action (Dec 2022) alleges breach of fiduciary duty and contribution with demand futility; defendants moved to dismiss. A consolidated EDNY securities class action alleges certain SEC filings were materially false or misleading regarding historical practices; defendants moved to dismiss the amended complaint.
  - Records preservation oversight: An EDNY derivative suit (Mar 2022) alleges breaches of fiduciary duty and securities law violations tied to SEC/CFTC resolutions; motion to dismiss the amended complaint is pending.
  - Oversight of banking services to Jeffrey Epstein: Two SDNY derivative suits (May/June 2023) alleging breaches of fiduciary duty and unjust enrichment by the Board and James Dimon; consolidated; defendants moved to dismiss the amended complaint.
- Broader legal posture and reserves: The Firm is involved in numerous additional proceedings, believes it has meritorious defenses, and intends to defend vigorously. It has established reserves for several hundred matters, accruing when losses are probable and estimable under U.S. GAAP; reserves are reassessed quarterly. Legal expense was $420 million for Q2 2023 versus $73 million for Q2 2022. While the Firm currently believes pending matters should not have a material adverse effect on consolidated financial condition (considering reserves and estimated possible losses), outcomes are uncertain and could exceed reserves and/or have reputational impacts; particular-period results could be materially affected depending on outcomes and earnings levels.
- Note 27 – Business segments: The Firm manages and reports on five segments: Consumer & Community Banking (CCB), Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB), Commercial Banking (CB), Asset & Wealth Management (AWM), and Corporate. Results are presented on a managed, FTE tax-equivalent basis, with reconciling items to U.S. GAAP. Capital allocation across lines of business is reviewed at least annually and was updated as of June 30, 2023 to reflect the First Republic acquisition.
- Segment results (three months ended June 30, 2023 vs 2022; managed basis):
  - Firmwide: Total net revenue $41.3B vs $30.7B; provision for credit losses $2.90B vs $1.10B; noninterest expense $20.8B vs $18.7B; net income $14.47B vs $8.65B; ROE 20% vs 13%; overhead ratio 50 vs 61; total assets $3.87T.
  - CCB: Net revenue $17.23B; provision $1.86B; noninterest expense $8.31B; net income $5.31B; ROE 38%; total assets $620.2B.
  - CIB: Net revenue $12.52B; provision $38M; noninterest expense $6.89B; net income $4.09B; ROE 15%; total assets $1.43T.
  - CB: Net revenue $3.99B; provision $1.10B; noninterest expense $1.30B; net income $1.21B; ROE 16%; total assets $305.3B.
  - AWM: Net revenue $4.94B; provision $145M; noninterest expense $3.16B; net income $1.23B; ROE 29%; total assets $247.1B.
  - Corporate: Net revenue $3.72B; provision $(243)M; noninterest expense $1.15B; net income $2.64B; total assets $1.26T.
  - Reconciling items eliminate FTE tax adjustments to arrive at reported U.S. GAAP; reconciling net income is zero.

text:
Shareholder Litigation . Several shareholder putative class 
actions, as well as shareholder derivative actions purporting 
to act on behalf of the Firm, have been filed against the 
Firm, its Board of Directors and certain of its current and 
former officers.  
Certain of these shareholder suits relate to historical 
trading practices by former employees in the precious 
metals and U.S. treasuries markets and related conduct 
which were the subject of the Firm’s resolutions with the 
DOJ, CFTC and SEC in September 2020, and fiduciary 
activities that were separately the subject of a resolution 
between JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. and the OCC in 
November 2020. One of these shareholder derivative suits 
was filed in the Supreme Court of the State of New York in 
May 2022, asserting breach of fiduciary duty and unjust 
enrichment claims relating to the historical trading 
practices and related conduct and fiduciary activities which were the subject of the resolutions described above. In 
December 2022, the court granted defendants’ motion to 
dismiss this action in full, and in January 2023, the plaintiff 
filed a notice of appeal, which remains pending. A second 
shareholder derivative action was filed in the United States 
District Court for the Eastern District of New York in 
December 2022 relating to the historical trading practices 
and related conduct, which asserts breach of fiduciary duty 
and contribution claims and alleges that the shareholder is 
excused from making a demand to commence litigation 
because such a demand would have been futile. Defendants 
have moved to dismiss the complaint. In addition, a 
consolidated putative class action is pending in the United 
States District Court for the Eastern District of New York on 
behalf of shareholders who acquired shares of JPMorgan 
Chase common stock during the putative class period, 
alleging that certain SEC filings of the Firm were materially 
false or misleading because they did not disclose certain 
information relating to the historical trading practices and 
conduct. Defendants have moved to dismiss the amended 
complaint in this action. 
A separate shareholder derivative suit was filed in March 
2022 in the United States District Court for the Eastern 
District of New York asserting breaches of fiduciary duty 
and violations of federal securities laws based on the 
alleged failure of the Board of Directors to exercise 
adequate oversight over the Firm’s compliance with records 
preservation requirements which were the subject of 
resolutions between certain of the Firm’s subsidiaries and 
the SEC and the CFTC. Defendants’ motion to dismiss the 
amended complaint is pending.
Two shareholder derivative suits were filed in May and June 
2023, respectively, in the United States District Court for 
the Southern District of New York asserting breaches of 
fiduciary duty and unjust enrichment based on the alleged 
failure of the Board of Directors and James Dimon to 
exercise adequate oversight with respect to the Firm’s 
provision of banking services to Jeffrey Epstein. These 
actions allege that the shareholders are excused from 
making a demand to commence litigation because such a 
demand would have been futile. These actions were 
consolidated and defendants have moved to dismiss the 
amended complaint filed by the plaintiffs. 
*     *     *
In addition to the various legal proceedings discussed 
above, JPMorgan Chase and its subsidiaries are named as 
defendants or are otherwise involved in a substantial 
number of other legal proceedings. The Firm believes it has 
meritorious defenses to the claims asserted against it in its 
currently outstanding legal proceedings and it intends to 
defend itself vigorously. Additional legal proceedings may 
be initiated from time to time in the future.
The Firm has established reserves for several hundred of its 
currently outstanding legal proceedings. In accordance with 
the provisions of U.S. GAAP for contingencies, the Firm 
accrues for a litigation-related liability when it is probable 
190that such a liability has been incurred and the amount of 
the loss can be reasonably estimated. The Firm evaluates its 
outstanding legal proceedings each quarter to assess its 
litigation reserves, and makes adjustments in such reserves, 
upward or downward, as appropriate, based on 
management’s best judgment after consultation with 
counsel. The Firm’s legal expense was $420 million  and 
$73 million  for the three months ended June 30, 2023 and 
2022 , respectively. There is no assurance that the Firm’s 
litigation reserves will not need to be adjusted in the future. 
In view of the inherent difficulty of predicting the outcome 
of legal proceedings, particularly where the claimants seek 
very large or indeterminate damages, or where the matters 
present novel legal theories, involve a large number of 
parties or are in early stages of discovery, the Firm cannot 
state with confidence what will be the eventual outcomes of 
the currently pending matters, the timing of their ultimate 
resolution or the eventual losses, fines, penalties or 
consequences related to those matters. JPMorgan Chase 
believes, based upon its current knowledge and after 
consultation with counsel, consideration of the material 
legal proceedings described above and after taking into 
account its current litigation reserves and its estimated 
aggregate range of possible losses, that the other legal 
proceedings currently pending against it should not have a 
material adverse effect on the Firm’s consolidated financial 
condition. The Firm notes, however, that in light of the 
uncertainties involved in such proceedings, there is no 
assurance that the ultimate resolution of these matters will 
not significantly exceed the reserves it has currently 
accrued or that a matter will not have material reputational 
consequences. As a result, the outcome of a particular 
matter may be material to JPMorgan Chase’s operating 
results for a particular period, depending on, among other 
factors, the size of the loss or liability imposed and the level 
of JPMorgan Chase’s income for that period.

title: Business combinations - Introduction
heading: Note 28 – Business combinations
start_phrase: On M a y 1 , 2 0 2 3, JPMorgan Chase acquired certain assets and assumed certain liabilities of First Republic Bank (the "First Republic acquisition") from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (“FDIC”), as receiver, fo r $67.9 billion , resulting in an estimated bargain purchase gain of $2.7 billion recorded in other income.
summary: JPMorgan Chase’s May 1, 2023 acquisition of certain assets and liabilities of First Republic Bank from the FDIC (as receiver) was accounted for as a U.S. GAAP business combination measured at estimated fair value, resulting in an estimated $2.7 billion bargain purchase gain recorded in other income. Purchase price consideration totaled $67.9 billion, comprising $13.6 billion paid/due to the FDIC net of cash acquired, a five-year $50.0 billion secured Purchase Money Note at 3.4% (fair value $48.8 billion), $5.4 billion for settlement of a prior First Republic deposit and related transactions, and $15 million contingent consideration for shared-loss agreements. Assets acquired were $192.3 billion (including $152.3 billion loans, $30.3 billion securities, $1.5 billion core deposit and customer relationship intangibles, $675 million indemnification assets for shared-loss agreements), and liabilities assumed were $121.7 billion (including $87.5 billion deposits and $27.9 billion FHLB advances), yielding $70.6 billion net assets and the gain noted above. JPMorgan Chase and the FDIC entered into two shared-loss agreements: CSLA covering 80% of credit losses on certain commercial loans and OREO for 5 years with a subsequent 3-year recovery period, and SFSLA covering 80% of credit losses for 7 years on certain primary-residence mortgage and cooperative share loans; related indemnification assets are included in total assets. The $50 billion Purchase Money Note is secured by certain acquired loans and is prepayable. A prior $5 billion deposit placed by JPMorgan Chase on March 16, 2023 as part of a $30 billion consortium was effectively settled at closing, with the related allowance for credit losses released; the Firm repaid the remaining $25 billion to the consortium with accrued interest on May 9, 2023. Certain items were non-cash transactions, including issuance of the Purchase Money Note, settlement of the $5 billion deposit and $447 million of securities financing, and a $3.7 billion payable to the FDIC. Fair value estimates involved market-based assumptions (expected cash flows, discount rates) and may be adjusted during the measurement period, with final settlement with the FDIC permitted up to one year post-acquisition; forthcoming sections describe accounting policies for intangibles, shared-loss agreements and indemnification assets, the Purchase Money Note, and FHLB advances.
text:
Business combinations 
On M a y  1 ,  2 0 2 3, JPMorgan Chase acquired certain assets 
and assumed certain liabilities of First Republic Bank (the 
"First Republic acquisition") from the Federal Deposit 
Insurance Corporation (“FDIC”), as receiver, fo r $67.9 
billion , resulting in an estimated  bargain purchase gain of 
$2.7 billion  recorded in other income. The estimated 
bargain purchase gain represents the excess of the 
estimated fair value of the net assets acquired above the 
purchase price. T he First Republic acquisition further 
advances  the Firm's wealth management  strategy and  is 
complementary to  the Firm's existing franchises.
The Firm has determined that this acquisition constitutes a 
business combination under U.S. GAAP. Accordingly, the 
initial recognition of the assets acquired  and liabilities 
assumed were generally measured at their estimated fair 
values as of  M a y  1 ,  2 0 2 3. The determination of those fair 
values required management to make certain market-based 
assumptions about expected future cash flows, discount 
rates and other valuation inputs at the time of the 
acquisition.  The Firm believes th at the fair value estimates 
of the assets acquired and liabilities assumed provide a 
reasonable basis for determining the estimated bargain 
purchase gain.  
The Firm and the FDIC have not yet completed the 
settlement process under which the purchase price, and the 
identification of the assets acquired and liabilities assumed, 
will be finalized. The finalization of this settlement process 
may impact the amount of the estimated bargain purchase 
gain. The purchase and assumption agreement entered into 
with the FDIC allows for final settlement to occur up to a 
year after the acquisition date . 
In addition, t he purchase price and the estimated bargain  
purchase gain could change pending management's 
finalization of its acquisition date fair value estimates for 
certain of the assets acquired and liabilities assumed ( such 
as loans and commitments, intangible assets and leases),  
which may take place up to one  year from the acquisition 
date , as permitted by U.S. GAAP.
In connection with the First Republic acquisition,  the Firm 
and the FDIC entered into two shared-loss agreements with 
respect to certain loans and lending-related commitments 
(the "shared-loss assets"): the Commercial Shared-Loss 
Agreement ("CSLA") and the Single-Family Shared-Loss 
Agreement (“SFSLA”). The CSLA covers  80%  of credit 
losses, on a pari-passu basis, over  5 years  with a 
subsequent  3-year  recovery period for certain acquired 
commercial loans and other real estate exposure. The 
SFSLA covers  80%  of credit losses, on a pari-passu basis, 
for 7 years  for certain acquired loans secured by mortgages 
on real property or shares in cooperative property 
constituting a primary residence . The indemnification assets 
which represent the fair value of the CSLA and SFSLA are 
reflected in the total assets acquired.As part of the consideration paid , JPMorgan Chase issued  a 
five-year , $50 billion  secured note to the FDIC (the 
"Purchase Money Note"). The Purchase Money Note bears 
interest at a fixed rate of  3.4%  and is secured by certain  of 
the acquired loans . The Purchase Money Note is prepayable 
upon notice to the FDIC.
The Firm had placed  a $5 billion  deposit with First Republic 
Bank on  M a r c h  1 6 ,  2 0 2 3, as part of  $30 billion  of deposits 
provided by a consortium of large U.S. banks.  The Firm's $5 
billion  deposit was effectively settled  as part of the 
acquisition and the associated allowance for credit losses 
was released upon closing.  The Firm  subsequently  repaid 
the remaining  $25 billion  of deposits  to the consortium of 
banks, including accrued interest  through the payment date 
on M a y  9 ,  2 0 2 3.

text:
Core deposit and customer relationship intangibles
Core deposit and certain wealth management customer 
relationship intangibles were acquired as part of the First 
Republic transaction. The core deposit intangible of  $1.3 
billion  was valued by discounting estimated after-tax cost 
savings over the remaining useful life of the deposits using 
the favorable source of funds method. The after-tax cost 
savings w ere estimated based on the difference between 
the cost of maintaining the core deposit base relative to the 
cost of next best alternative funding sources available to 
market participants. The customer relationship intangibles 
of $187 million  were  valued by discounting estimated after-
tax earnings over their remaining useful lives using the 
multi-period excess earnings method. Both intangible asset 
valuations utilized assumptions  that the Firm believes a 
market participant would use to estimate fair values , such 
as gr owth and attrition rate s, projected fee income as well as related costs to service the relationships, and discount 
rates. The core deposit and customer relationship 
intangibles will be amortized over a projected period of 
future cash flows of approximately  7 years . As of June 30, 
2023, the carrying values of the core deposit and customer 
relationship intangibles were  $1.2 billion  and $183 million , 
respectively , reflecting accumulated amortization of 
approximately  $30 million  and $4 million , respectively .

  - Lending-related commitments $2.4 billion

- Accounting policies and valuation methodologies for key items:
  - Core deposit and customer relationship intangibles:
    - Core deposit intangible of $1.3 billion valued using a favorable source of funds method (discounted after-tax cost savings)
    - Customer relationship intangibles of $187 million valued using the multi-period excess earnings method
    - Assumptions include growth/attrition, projected fee income, servicing costs, and discount rates
    - Amortized over about 7 years; as of June 30, 2023, carrying values were $1.2 billion (core) and $183 million (customer), with accumulated amortization of ~$30 million and $4 million, respectively

    - Indemnification assets recorded at fair value based on timing and amount of forecasted losses tied to the allowance for credit losses; remeasured quarterly through other income
    - Potential future FDIC payment upon termination reflected as contingent consideration
  - Purchase Money Note and FHLB advances valued using discounted cash flow approaches with market-based rates; PM Note recorded in long-term debt; FHLB advances recorded in short-term borrowings and long-term debt

text:
Indemnification assets - Shared-loss agreements
The indemnification assets represent forecasted recoveries 
from the FDIC associated with the shared-loss assets over 
the respective shared loss recovery periods. The 
indemnification assets were recorded at fair value in other 
assets on the Consolidated balance sheets on the 
acquisition date. The fair values of the indemnification 
assets were estimated based on the timing of the forecasted 
losses underlying the related allowance for credit losses.  
195The subsequent quarterly remeasurement of the 
indemnification assets will be based on changes in amount 
and timing of forecasted losses in the allowance for credit 
losses associated with the shared loss assets and will be 
recorded in other income. Under certain circumstances,  the 
Firm may be required to make a payment to the FDIC upon 
termination of the shared-loss agreements based on the 
level of actual losses and recoveries on the shared-loss 
assets. The estimated potential future payment is reflected 
as contingent consideration as part of the purchase price 
consideration.

The Purchase Money Note is recorded in long-term debt on

discount rates.  
The FHLB advances assumed in the acquisition are recorded

value of the FHLB advances was based on a discounted cash 
flow methodology and  considered the observed FHLB 
advance issuance rates.

summary:
- Presents JPMorgan Chase’s unaudited consolidated average balance sheets, interest, and annualized rates on a taxable-equivalent basis (in millions) for:
  - Three months ended June 30, 2023 vs. 2022
  - Six months ended June 30, 2023 vs. 2022
- Details average balances, interest income/expense, and yields/costs by major asset categories:
  - Deposits with banks, federal funds sold and securities purchased under resale agreements, securities borrowed
  - Trading assets – debt instruments
  - Investment securities (taxable and nontaxable)
  - Loans
  - All other interest-earning assets
- Details average balances, interest expense, and costs by major liability categories:
  - Interest-bearing deposits, federal funds purchased and securities loaned/sold under repurchase agreements
  - Short-term borrowings (incl. commercial paper)
  - Trading liabilities – debt and other interest-bearing liabilities
  - Beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs
  - Long-term debt
  - Also shows noninterest-bearing deposits, trading liabilities (equity and derivative payables), and other liabilities
- Provides totals for average assets, liabilities, and stockholders’ equity (preferred and common)
- Reports interest rate spread, net interest income (NII), and net yield on interest-earning assets:
  - Q2 2023: NII $21.9B; net yield 2.62%; spread 1.97% vs. Q2 2022: NII $15.2B; net yield 1.80%; spread 1.68%
  - 1H 2023: NII $42.7B; net yield 2.63%; spread 2.00% vs. 1H 2022: NII $29.2B; net yield 1.74%; spread 1.64%
- Highlights notable YoY shifts:
  - Higher asset yields across categories (e.g., loans ~6.6% vs. ~4.3% in Q2) and materially higher funding costs (interest-bearing deposits ~2.24% vs. ~0.20% in Q2)
  - Average loans up; deposits with banks and noninterest-bearing deposits down; long-term debt higher
  - Total interest-earning assets modestly lower YoY in Q2; mix shifts in trading assets/liabilities
- Includes footnotes on:
  - Tax-exempt treatment of certain securities; impact of related hedging derivatives on interest
  - Amortized cost-based securities yields vs. fair value changes in AOCI
  - Classification details (e.g., brokerage-related receivables/payables, inclusion of commercial paper)
  - Combined balances for trading liabilities – debt and equity instruments
- Appends a Glossary of Terms and Acronyms defining key items used (e.g., AFS, AOCI, CECL, CET1, VIEs, CIB, AWM, ABS, CDS, criticized, CVA, etc.)
